commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

(claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

# INDEX_RULES.md — Global Rules & Doc Routing

**Doc link:** <https://github.com/brando90/agents-config/blob/main/INDEX_RULES.md>

**TLDR:** Read this compact contract at task start, then read only the detailed rule sections whose triggers apply. All agents use the same policy; client-specific loading differs.

## How to load these rules

Refresh `~/agents-config` with `git -C ~/agents-config pull --ff-only` at each new non-trivial task and after an hour; preserve dirty/concurrent work and use the local copy if offline. Reread this index and relevant changed rules. When editing agents-config in an isolated checkout, use that checkout's index and detail files after refreshing the home checkout.

All Hard Rule **Details** links and matching Trigger Rule/Guideline links are mandatory routing: **before the action they govern, read that detail section and its applicable workflow**, including secret overrides, spending and review decisions. Do not read every topic file. Rule numbers are stable; paths below resolve beneath `~/agents-config/` (or the active agents-config checkout). If files are unavailable locally, fetch the same path under `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brando90/agents-config/main/`. A Markdown link is a reading instruction, not proof the client loaded it. Never eagerly import this index or the detail collection into an entry file; read them as task files.

Hard rules govern conflicts with older wording in a triggered procedure. Explicit user instructions and platform/tool constraints retain their normal precedence. The SNAP pre-approval in Trigger Rule 51 is scoped to authorized work and existing budgets. Detail pages retain the procedures, examples and exceptions; the catalog is optional lookup.

## Hard Rules (every response, never skip)

1. **Protect secrets.** Never commit credentials; inspect the exact staged diff and filenames before committing or pushing. Do not print secret values. Stop on a suspected leak and rotate exposed credentials; references/env vars replace embedded secrets. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-1)

2. **Sync, then verify before pushing.** `git fetch` first; if upstream moved, rebase and re-test; never force-push a shared branch. Never fabricate unavailable source content; mark it unresolved. Inspect the diff and run the relevant deterministic checks. Report actual evidence and limitations, not an untested success claim. [Details](rules/maintenance.md#hard-rule-2)

3. **Quality assurance (QA) is opt-in.** Only a tier Brando explicitly requests or sets for this work in a runbook, `[qa]`/`[light-qa]`/`[mega-qa]` commit tag or environment flag starts a model reviewer. Hooks, project files and older “QA required” text are not opt-in. “Do QA”/“light QA” means one opposite-company round; apply findings and verify without automatic re-review. Mega QA follows Trigger Rule 10. Hooks cannot impose unsolicited QA; do not mention QA when unrequested. Benchmark-reference acceptance (43) remains separate. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-3)

4. **Response ending and titles.** Compact results: 1–2 sentences plus `.md`/`gdoc` links. End `**TLDR-end:** [proj: task]` with 1–2 sentences (`[proj]` without a task); never open `TLDR-start`. Emails/status reports also end `TLDR-end:` before any signature; include real decisions/deadlines only. Name and restate the core deliverable, not a micro-step (optional `›` suffix). Research updates open with a copy-ready status sentence; results also include a 1–2 sentence collaborator message in Brando’s voice. Match owned titles to verified summaries, identifier first. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-4)

5. **Snapshot.** In chat, immediately after the closing summary, show `**Snapshot:**` with the smallest real artifact sample (normally 5–15 lines, at most 25), or say why nothing tangible exists. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-5)

6. **Refresh configuration.** Follow the task-start/hourly refresh above, reread relevant changes, and preserve other owners’ work. Shared edits belong in both entry points. Review remains opt-in under Hard Rule 3. [Details](rules/maintenance.md#hard-rule-6)

7. **Keep clients current.** Use the installed package manager and the supported update hook; never assume npm. Do not install/use the deprecated Gemini CLI. [Details](rules/maintenance.md#hard-rule-7)

8. **Models, budgets and acceptance.** Masters: Codex `gpt-6-astra` / `ultra`; Claude `claude-fable-5-1` / `max`. Keep configured defaults; explicitly select proportionate execution workers (experiment selection: Guideline 19). Verify actual models/efforts and billing route (subscription or in-scope provider key). Never buy credits, enable new charges or weaken acceptance to recover. Required models/families and scientific pins remain binding. Before dispatch/review, read this detail and Rule 48. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-8)

9. **Model access: CLIs, subscriptions and provider keys are allowed.** Agents may wire Brando's existing provider keys into agent clients, write provider application programming interface (API) calls and run key-loading scripts without asking. Load keys at runtime, never print or commit them, keep each within its owner's scope and existing budgets, and cap and cost-estimate key-billed batch or unattended runs. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-9)

10. **Explain terminology.** Expand every acronym, metric symbol and project-specific term on first use in each response, chat included; use descriptive names, not opaque internal labels. For Brando, a code may lead if a short gloss follows on first use. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-10)

11. **Numbers with verdicts.** Compact entries link full statistics (Rule 4). Give measured values, scales, denominators/splits, threshold sources, missing measurements. Statistical headlines need 95% intervals (resampling unit, limits) and `x [lo, hi] p-val=Z` (named test/null or `p-val=n/a`). Report correlations individually; when interpreting score levels, add absolute agreement and mean bias (judge minus human, positive = lenient) with both means. Give repeated-score variability/counts. Existing data only; read the statistics workflow first. Research precision (10-24-2026): read settings, definitions, numbers from the repo, run records or paper; `unknown` only after a named-path search (in caption). VeriBench tables carry a Pi + best open-weight row. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-11)

## Guidelines (best practices)

- [14](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-14): Complete direct authorized requests; do not ask again for already-authorized actions.
- [15](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-15): Read only task-relevant referenced docs.
- [16](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-16): Keep index, README and paths accurate; mirror shared entry bodies; verify actual host instruction files and reload state.
- [17](rules/responses.md#guideline-rule-17): Use anchored paths in prose and commands.
- [18](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-18): Use `ls -la` for configuration/credential directories.
- [19](rules/research.md#guideline-rule-19): Select experiment models/judges by capability, total cost and validation; preserve pins.
- [20](rules/responses.md#guideline-rule-20): Messages/drafts as Brando use his concise first-person voice; email includes required routing/signature.
- [21](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-21): Check `~/keys/` for credentials, model-provider keys included, before asking; keep values transient.
- [22](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-22): Let the Node version manager control its path; avoid hardcoded versioned PATH entries.
- [23](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-23): Authorized email: Brando's signed-in account (mail connector, else uutils SMTP); BCC three inboxes, sender and To included; visible CC only on request; `drafted with <agent>` sign-off; “send” means send.
- [24](rules/maintenance.md#guideline-rule-24): Paper PDFs follow mandatory Rule 35.
- [25](rules/research.md#guideline-rule-25): VeriBench/VB private: >0.98 saturated; ≤0.9 good, ≤0.5 great, 0 best. "Harsh metric", N tasks, ASCII, harness. vb-priv: SYNC.md. Any metric ≥~0.98: solved (heuristic). [Set names](workflows/vb-sets.md).

## Authorized sign-in and verification codes

For an authorized account task, read [Rule 34](rules/services.md#trigger-rule-34): verify account, existing session or matching saved login and current challenge codes; keep credentials transient. Sign-in does not authorize unrelated transactions or messages.

## Machine Configs

Host routes: [catalog](CATALOG.md#machine-configs): [Mac](machine/mac.md), [SNAP](machine/snap.md), [Sherlock](machine/sherlock-agent-access.md), [FarmShare](machine/farmshare.md), [other agent clients](machine/agent-clis.md). Do not load unrelated hosts.

## Workflows

Use matching trigger links first. The [workflow catalog](CATALOG.md#workflows) indexes detailed procedures; [instruction maintenance](docs/instruction-audit/README.md) records the size budgets and client compatibility.

## Writing

The [writing catalog](CATALOG.md#writing) routes paper, blog and announcement work. Colocate all artifacts for a project/event; do not split them into top-level directories by file type.

## Abbreviations

`ac` = agents-config; `cc` = Claude Code. [Launcher/profile aliases](rules/services.md#abbreviations) are labels, not proof of account access or independent budget.

## Collaborators / Contact roster

Before addressing/assigning a person, resolve identity through [contacts](personal/contacts.md) and the [roster route](rules/services.md#collaborators--contact-roster).

## SNAP watcher reauth & reboot persistence (2026-04)

[Watcher reference](rules/hosts.md#snap-watcher-reauth--reboot-persistence-2026-04).

Research updates open with a copy-ready status sentence; results also include a 1–2 sentence collaborator message in Brando’s voice. Match owned titles to verified summaries, identifier first. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-4)

5. **Snapshot.** In chat, immediately after the closing summary, show `**Snapshot:**` with the smallest real artifact sample (normally 5–15 lines, at most 25), or say why nothing tangible exists. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-5)

6. **Refresh configuration.** Follow the task-start/hourly refresh above, reread relevant changes, and preserve other owners’ work. Shared edits belong in both entry points. Review remains opt-in under Hard Rule 3. [Details](rules/maintenance.md#hard-rule-6)

7. **Keep clients current.** Use the installed package manager and the supported update hook; never assume npm. Do not install/use the deprecated Gemini CLI. [Details](rules/maintenance.md#hard-rule-7)

8. **Models, budgets and acceptance.** Masters: Codex `gpt-6-astra` / `ultra`; Claude `claude-fable-5-1` / `max`. Keep configured defaults; explicitly select proportionate execution workers (experiment selection: Guideline 19). Verify actual models/efforts and billing route (subscription or in-scope provider key). Never buy credits, enable new charges or weaken acceptance to recover. Required models/families and scientific pins remain binding. Before dispatch/review, read this detail and Rule 48. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-8)

9. **Model access: CLIs, subscriptions and provider keys are allowed.** Agents may wire Brando's existing provider keys into agent clients, write provider application programming interface (API) calls and run key-loading scripts without asking. Load keys at runtime, never print or commit them, keep each within its owner's scope and existing budgets, and cap and cost-estimate key-billed batch or unattended runs. [Details](rules/safety-and-models.md#hard-rule-9)

10. **Explain terminology.** Expand every acronym, metric symbol and project-specific term on first use in each response, chat included; use descriptive names, not opaque internal labels. For Brando, a code may lead if a short gloss follows on first use. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-10)

11. **Numbers with verdicts.** Compact entries link full statistics (Rule 4). Give measured values, scales, denominators/splits, threshold sources, missing measurements. Statistical headlines need 95% intervals (resampling unit, limits) and `x [lo, hi] p-val=Z` (named test/null or `p-val=n/a`). Report correlations individually; when interpreting score levels, add absolute agreement and mean bias (judge minus human, positive = lenient) with both means. Give repeated-score variability/counts. Existing data only; read the statistics workflow first. Research precision (10-24-2026): read settings, definitions, numbers from the repo, run records or paper; `unknown` only after a named-path search (in caption). VeriBench tables carry a Pi + best open-weight row. [Details](rules/responses.md#hard-rule-11)

content.content:
## Hard Rule 3

3. **QA is explicit opt-in: run it only when Brando asks for it.** QA here means a model-reviewer pass (quality assurance, QA). It runs only when Brando explicitly requests a tier -- "do QA" / "QA it" / "light QA" (one review round), "mega QA" and the other Trigger Rule 10 phrases (the sequential chain) -- or when a runbook or commit tag he set names the tier (for example `[mega-qa]`). No agent starts a reviewer on its own: not for code, shared rules, claims/results, pushes to `main`, end-of-day or "high-stakes" moments, and not because a hook, a project file or an older rule text says QA is "required". **No repo-level hook may force QA on push** (Brando, 2026-09-15: "no repo in my computer should be doing a qa automatically"): a `git push` / `gh pr merge` gate in `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/hooks/*`, `.git/hooks/*` or CI must stay silent unless a tier was explicitly requested through an opt-in Brando set (env flag such as `<PROJ>_LIGHT_QA=1` / `<PROJ>_MEGA_QA=1`, or a `[qa]` / `[light-qa]` / `[mega-qa]` commit tag); a hook that blocks pushes by default is a bug to fix in that repo, not a rule to obey. **Without a request, still verify the work deterministically** before reporting done -- self-review the diff, `git diff --check`, and the relevant tests / compile / render / targeted grep. **Do not mention QA at all when none was requested** -- no "no QA was run" / "No QA was requested or run" line in replies, checkpoints or commit messages (Brando, 09-16-2026: "The default if qa's aren't the default is to not mention them at all"; the earlier "say in the reply that no QA was run" clause made every reply carry that sentence and was removed). **When QA is requested:** "do QA" or "light QA" = ONE opposite-agent round (Claude Code built -> Codex reviews; Codex built -> Claude Code reviews), the builder applies the findings, verifies them with deterministic checks, done; no automatic re-review. A second round or more only if Brando asks ("otherwise I run out of tokens", 2026-08-20). "mega QA" = Trigger Rule 10. **Separate acceptance requirements are not QA and are unchanged:** benchmark reference (gold) edits still need both model families (Trigger Rule 43), and a scientific model pin or an explicitly required reviewer family stays binding. **Why:** Brando, 09-14-2026: "can we make the qa rule in ac always explicit. I need to say do qa, mega or light for it to be triggered." **CLI-only, no API keys.** Any reviewer dispatch must use locally logged-in approved CLIs (`codex`, `clauded`) with cached subscription/OAuth credentials; never fall back to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_API_KEY` / `GEMINI_API_KEY`. The deprecated Gemini CLI must not be used. Claude and Codex remain the preferred review families; Brando's September 11 cross-provider recovery authorization also permits other verified subscription clients under Trigger Rule 48 where the canonical review procedure allows them. Explicit required families and benchmark-reference acceptance are unchanged. See [`workflows/qa-correctness.md`](../workflows/qa-correctness.md) for tiers and [`workflows/qa-structural.md`](../workflows/qa-structural.md) for structural checks.

## Hard Rule 8

8. **Strong masters; proportionate execution workers; bounded review and quota recovery.** Keep the strongest configured model for masters and reasoning-critical work. A master explicitly chooses each worker's model and effort for its phase; capable regular workers are the default for well-specified execution. A detailed handoff reduces ambiguity, not the required standard of correctness. Do not lower global defaults to dispatch a worker. Trigger Rule 48 and [`workflows/reliable-agent-dispatch.md`](../workflows/reliable-agent-dispatch.md) define the completion budget, verified handoff and cross-provider recovery contract.
    - **Pinned defaults:** Codex `gpt-6-astra` with `model_reasoning_effort = "ultra"` in `~/.codex/config.toml`; dispatch with `codex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox -m gpt-6-astra -c 'model_reasoning_effort="ultra"' "$QA_PROMPT"`. Claude Code `claude-fable-5-1` with `"effortLevel": "max"` in `~/.claude/settings.json` ([template](../claude-code-settings.json)); dispatch with `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions --model claude-fable-5-1 --effort max` (`claude-fable-5-1[1m]` for the one-million-token context variant). For a review that must not edit, put that constraint in the review brief while retaining full launch access under Trigger Rule 51; `--full-auto` is removed. Follow Trigger Rule 42 for unattended worker permissions and isolation.
    - **Worker selection:** separate planning, routine execution, the model being measured, and acceptance review. Prefer direct commands for deterministic work; for bounded implementation or research with clear inputs/tests, select a regular reasoning worker and supported effort explicitly. Escalate difficult decisions to the master or a stronger worker based on evidence. Reserve shared subscription allowance for remaining work, reviews and publication; do not send every remote worker at the master's maximum effort. Record exact selected and actual settings, role, rationale and eligible substitutes under Rule 48.
    - **Reviewer selection:** prefer the strongest reviewer from the other company. For ordinary changes, if that model cannot run, try one suitable smaller reasoning model from that company before a fresh strongest-model review from the builder's company. Default chain (3 stages, preferred Claude/Codex chain; any eligible substitute follows the canonical review procedure and Rule 48): Codex → CC → Codex (if CC built) or CC → Codex → CC (if Codex built) — the builder reviews in the middle (knows intent best); the non-builder CLI takes the first and last (clean-eyes) passes in fresh contexts. If the user asks for more rounds, cycle the chain in fresh contexts. **Per-stage fallback:** apply Hard Rule 8 and the canonical [review fallback procedure](../workflows/qa-correctness.md#review-fallback-and-acceptance). Complete the planned stages using eligible reviewers; an advisory smaller-model pass cannot fill a stage requiring a strongest-model reviewer. Preserve mandatory cross-company checks, including Trigger Rule 43. If no eligible reviewer can run, stop and report the incomplete stage; never claim acceptance from stage count alone. **Manual-only (Brando 2026-08-20):** the mega chain runs only when Brando himself types a trigger; an agent must never choose it on its own — not for end-of-day, pre-merge, pre-sleep, or "high-stakes" moments. 43. **Benchmark reference ("gold") data is built, repaired and checked with BOTH model families at their top tier -- never one model alone.** _Trigger: you create, repair, relabel, re-prove, or review the reference side of a benchmark -- gold solutions, ground-truth specifications or theorem statements, gold labels, oracle outputs (expected reference answers), or any dataset that scores are measured against -- for VeriBench or any other benchmark._ Use the smartest current Codex model **and** the smartest current Claude Code model (whichever model identifiers (IDs) Hard Rule 8 names today) on every reference change: no gold edit is accepted on one family's judgment alone -- the other family must have checked it (reviewed the edit, or independently reproduced the result) before it lands. Reference data is the one experiment input exempt from Hard Rule 8's regular "workload" tier: it is correctness-critical, so both models run at the flagship tier (the strongest model tier), while the agent-under-test, the evaluation judge and bulk generation keep following Hard Rule 8 and Guideline 19. Record which model produced and which model checked each landed change (Guideline 19's model-ID requirement, applied per edit). If one family's command-line interface (CLI) is quota-blocked, Hard Rule 8's switch to the other CLI still applies to *continuing the work* (proposing edits, running compiles), but *acceptance* waits until the other family has checked the edit; note the wait in `results.md`.

    **How to apply:** the recommended shape is the VeriBench phase-2 repair driver `~/veribench/experiments/75_gold_sorry_closure/scripts/repair_gold_reference.sh` (on branch `expt75-repair-driver`, which is where these files live until they land on `main`; check it out in a worktree you own -- `~/veribench-wt-expt75` was the original one and no longer exists): `PROVERS=codex,claude`, the two provers alternate per file behind a mechanical guard, the non-proposing model is the adversarial reviewer (it actively searches for errors in the proposed edit) (`scripts/prompts/repair_prover.md` / `repair_reviewer.md` beside it), and the ledger names both models per edit. Rotating the proposer and logging attribution are the implementation, not extra mandates: any design in which both families at the top tier sign off on every landed reference edit satisfies the rule. Start a new benchmark's reference set from that shape rather than from a one-model pipeline.

55:16. **Document headers: title, clickable document address, then summary.** _Trigger: you create a new document or substantially rewrite one (any `.md`, `.txt`, `.rst`; design docs, plans, READMEs, reports, summaries, postmortems, eval writeups)._ The first non-blank line of the file MUST be a `# Title` heading describing the doc's purpose, followed by a `**TLDR:**` block of 1–2 sentences summarizing the document (after the document link when applicable). ## Hard Rule 4

4. **TLDR at the end.** Every response must end with a `**TLDR-end:**` line — 1–2 sentences — written last, from the actual response content, so it reflects any conclusion that changed along the way. Do not open responses with a `**TLDR-start:**` line; Brando retired the opening TLDR on 2026-09-14. **Project tag:** prefix the TLDR with a square-bracket tag in the format `[proj: task]` — **project first**, then the current task; if there is no clear task yet, project only: `[proj]`. Use a concise/abbreviated project name (e.g. `vb` for veribench, `beyond-scale`) — e.g. `**TLDR-end:** [vb: leap-gemini-key] …` — so Brando can tell which project/conversation a response belongs to from the TLDR alone (he reviews many per day and otherwise cannot place them). Lean on the project as the anchor. Keep the whole tag short, and outside the 1–2 sentence budget.

   **Core-work reminder (Brando, 10-05-2026).** "Remind me what the most relevant/recent task you are doing (like important core experiment I mean, not small things like 'test arg', more like 'generating outputs with FMs for human judgements') … at the very least in the tldrs." The task part of the tag names the core experiment or deliverable the conversation is pursuing (what Brando would write in his weekly document), not the current micro-step; it changes only when the core work changes. A sub-step may follow `›`, for example `[vb: expt106 fake-human panel, leave-one-agent-out judge test › Argon smoke test]`. The TLDR's first clause restates that core work in plain words before the step's result, so a reader who sees only the TLDR knows which real experiment is running. Applies to all agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.). No exceptions.

   **Copy-ready weekly-update sentence (Brando, 09-24-2026).** For substantial research or experiment updates, open with one plain, self-contained sentence that Brando can paste directly into his weekly Google Doc: aim for one rendered line, two at most, matching the brevity of the approved example below. Include the experiment, essential setup and current result/status; omit secondary settings and operational details. Use current verified facts, and keep pending results explicit. This opening sentence has no heading or `TLDR-start` label; retain the closing `TLDR-end` and Snapshot protocol.

   Approved example: Experiment 95: 896 VeriBench tasks via Valkyrie; Terminus2 + GPT-6 Luna solver, GPT-6 Sol judge (both high reasoning); results pending.

   **Task titles match copy-ready summaries (Brando, 09-25-2026).** Name each agent/chat/task with the same self-contained, one-sentence summary used in Brando's tracking document: project or experiment identifier, concrete scope/setup (including solver/judge models and effort when relevant), and latest verified outcome or unresolved goal. Keep the identifier first so truncated sidebars remain recognizable. Prefer the full sentence when supported; if a hard title limit applies, preserve identifier, distinguishing setup and status, and keep the full sentence in the task's first summary/checkpoint. Refresh the title when scope or material status changes; never imply the research goal is achieved merely because a run ended. Do not rename unrelated tasks speculatively. Agents own their title updates using their own evidence. Propagate rule changes with one brief notice at the next safe boundary: no worker interruption/restart, repeated acknowledgments, or changes to experiment settings/schedulers.

   Approved title example: Experiment 95: 896 VeriBench tasks via Valkyrie; Terminus2 + GPT-6 Luna solver, GPT-6 Sol judge (both high reasoning); 881 compiled, judging failed, saturation unresolved.

**Compact results entries (Brando, 10-15-2026).** For a task-list result, weekly-update item or chat result summary, use **1–2 sentences plus two links**: state the finding with its decisive numbers and scope, then the material limitation or consequence. Finish with `Table:` and verified links labeled `.md` and `gdoc`. Keep full methods, uncertainty, factor tables and execution history in the linked reports. Do not expand a short result entry into the full-report template. If a requested link is unavailable, say so briefly; never invent one. See [the exact format](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#compact-results-entry).

**Copy-ready collaborator message (Brando, 10-16-2026).** Whenever giving Brando research results, also include one **1–2 sentence message in Brando’s voice** that he can copy to Sanmi or the intended collaborator. Label it `Copy-ready message` outside the draft text. Use natural first-person wording where appropriate, scientific but easy to read; improve clarity without making his voice stiff or dense. Infer the audience from the conversation rather than always addressing Sanmi. State the main finding, enough scope and decisive numbers to interpret it, and the caveat or consequence that changes the takeaway. Distinguish measured results from hypotheses; preserve uncertainty and avoid causal overclaims.

Give one draft by default, not several alternatives. Keep internal paths, operational details, full statistical tables and chat-only closing blocks outside the copied message; relevant report links may accompany it. This message supplements the result summary and linked Markdown/Google reports, and is distinct from the opening weekly-update status sentence. It applies to research results, not routine administrative updates. Drafting does not authorize sending a message.

## Hard Rule 10

10. **Expand every acronym and define every piece of jargon on FIRST USE, in every response.** Applies to ordinary chat replies, not just to papers and reader-facing prose. The first time an abbreviation, initialism, or project-specific term appears in a response, write it out and say what it means in one short clause: `TBH (to be honest)`, `SCSC (Smooth Conjunctive Score for Code verification)`, `IC_pp (fraction of the agent's stated theorems it actually proved)`, `the fresh re-run` (rather than an in-house label like "Arm 2" that means nothing outside the experiment folder). Casual abbreviations count: `tbh`, `iirc`, `afaict`, `wrt`, `ETA`, `EOD`. So do metric symbols, factor names, experiment-internal vocabulary, file/label identifiers, and any term whose meaning depends on a document the reader is not currently looking at. Use the expansion once, then the short form freely for the rest of that response; re-expand in the next response, since Brando may be reading it on its own. **The trap this closes:** an agent reads an experiment README or a results summary, absorbs its private vocabulary, and then writes as if that vocabulary were shared -- but Brando is reading the reply, not the file the agent just read. **Why:** stated by Brando 2026-09-02 after a reply built an entire analysis on the in-house labels "Arm 1" / "Arm 2" without ever saying what they meant, leaving him to ask whether it meant the ARM hardware architecture. **Borrowed metaphors are jargon too:** "arm" there was the clinical-trial sense (one branch of an experiment), which is useless to a reader who is not running clinical trials -- the fix was not to define it but to rename it to what it actually was, a rescore of old runs versus a fresh re-run: "tell me what acronyms mean. I don't know what you're talking about" and "otherwise I don't know what the fuck you're talking about in your responses agents!" An unexplained acronym silently transfers the agent's work onto the reader. **Distinct from Trigger Rules 23 and 24**, which govern jargon in *reader-facing prose* (papers, blog posts); this Hard Rule governs every response the agent writes, to anyone, including Brando.

    **Codes carry a gloss (Brando, 10-13-2026).** In anything Brando reads (chat, weekly-update text, to-do lines, email), a code-like name may lead and may be bold, but on its first use in a message or section it is followed by a short parenthetical saying what it is, the way agent task titles do: `**V21-008** (the SampCert task, first candidate for the private V2.1 set)`, `**1A** (raters qualify on the first warm-up task only)`, `**T01** (Rylan)`, `**C17** (the amendment that fixed that rule)`. Later mentions in the same message may use the bare bold code; a plain-words name with the code in parentheses is equally fine. What is never fine is a bare code with no gloss anywhere in the message. Agent-to-agent records (checkpoints, ledgers, commit messages) may keep bare codes. **Why:** Brando, 10-13-2026, reading "102 set-N round: 1A, 2A, 3A ... V21-008 D1-D3 ... V008-01 D1-D4": "too many acronyms ... for me as a human it's difficult to read"; then, on an all-plain-language reply: "We can use both. The bolded acronym like names is nice. Maybe it just needs a parenthesis with a small description or something? Like the agent tasks titles sort of have."

## Hard Rule 11

11. **Show measured numbers alongside verdicts.** In every response or report, accompany pass/fail, accepted/rejected, threshold outcomes and qualitative judgments with the actual measured numerical results that support them; a verdict such as "none passed" alone hides how good the results are. Give clear metric names, units or scales, sample counts/denominators, the data split or phase, and uncertainty when available. For correlation analyses, report Pearson, Spearman and Kendall individually when available. When a score's value is itself interpreted (a level, threshold, "saturated" or a mapped scale), add one absolute-agreement statistic, such as ICC(A,1) or mean absolute error with mean bias, because correlations cannot show a constant offset; define bias with its sign every time, as the mean of (judge or model score minus the human or reference score), so a positive bias means the judge is lenient, and give the two means it comes from (Brando, 10-02-2026). Uncertainty, both always: give a 95% interval for every headline estimate, saying what was resampled (tasks, items, repeats) and what the interval does not cover, and add a p-value whenever a verdict is read from the number, against a named null (a zero difference, or the pre-declared threshold such as a 0.45 agreement gate or a 0.8 saturation line), naming the test; do not report p-values against "correlation is zero", which are uninformative, and write every interval as x [lo, hi] followed by p-val=Z naming the test, or p-val=n/a when no test was run (Brando, 10-02-2026). Full results reports follow the detailed example in [`workflows/statistics-reporting.md`](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#detailed-report-example-brando-10-02-2026): hypothesis as a question plus the metric, instrument with train/val/test agreement, results per system, a verdict bullet against the pre-declared threshold, a next step. For repeated scoring, report standard deviations and repetition counts, distinguishing variability across raw repeated scores from repeatability of aggregated scores (state what was aggregated and how). Compute these from data the experiment already has: this rule never requires extra runs, seeds, model calls or human labels, and a statistic the data cannot support is reported as "single run" or unavailable. Prefer cheap, honest reuse of that data to estimate uncertainty and variance, such as a bootstrap or permutation test over the independent unit (tasks or seeds, not correlated items within them) or statistics over repeats already made, and name the method. Validating a judge or proxy against human labels follows the [judge-human agreement checklist](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#judge-human-agreement-checklist); both tiers, with reasons, are in [`workflows/statistics-reporting.md`](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md). "Raw numbers" means actual measured values, including useful summaries, not a dump of every observation. Mark missing metrics **unavailable** or **not measured**, never invent them. Show thresholds as secondary context and identify their source: user-chosen, protocol-defined or agent-suggested. A promising starting point is not an acceptance gate; this reporting rule never changes scientific protocols, results, thresholds or scoring. **Why:** Brando, 09-15-2026, asked to see the numbers behind judge-validation verdicts, not just whether they cleared a threshold. On 09-30-2026 a VeriBench judge with Pearson 0.86 still scored 0.18 above expert raters on average, which correlations alone could not show; Brando then asked that the rule stay cheap and general across training, reinforcement-learning and judge experiments.

**Presentation exception for compact result entries (10-15-2026).** Hard Rule 11 still governs the underlying evidence. In the 1–2 sentence format above, give the decisive values and denominator/scope, and put the full confidence intervals, resampling unit, p-value or `p-val=n/a`, mean bias, repeated-score variability and provenance in the two linked reports. Keep uncertainty in the short entry whenever omitting it would change the verdict. This is a brevity rule, not permission to imply an unmeasured result or unsupported generalization.

**Research precision: search before "unknown" (Brando, 10-24-2026).** Research and science have to be precise, and Brando should never need to remind an agent of this ("like we should never need a reminder like this ... Is research/science! it has to be precise man"; "I'd much rather you search the repo always to give me the accurate setting than saying idk"). Before any model setting (model ID, effort, thinking mode, checkpoint, quantization, serving engine and version, sampling settings, harness and its config), judge, definition, version, count or score goes into a table, caption, note or message, read it from the project's own records: the repo, experiment READMEs and protocols, run configs and launch scripts, receipts, saved run records and logs, the paper and its support files, `git log`/`git grep` including open pull requests, and the run's host when the record lives only there (fetch it; a setting that sits on a cluster is not unknown). Write `unknown` only after that search comes up empty, and have the caption name the paths searched; never write "idk", never guess, never ask Brando for something the repo could answer. Missing values stay unknown or a range, never zero. Every run records its settings in the project's GitHub experiment notes when it starts, so no later result says unknown because the setting sits on a cluster. Tables keep harness and model as separate columns. When two sources disagree, name the disagreement and use the primary one (the paper for definitions, saved run records for settings). Each project's `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` carries this rule near the top; VeriBench's full text is `docs/agent_rules/research_precision.md` in the veribench repo.

**Pi + best open-weight row in every VeriBench table (Brando, 10-24-2026: "can we always have at least 1 pi + best open source model we can run for this table? (or the full data set table too) Go run it if it's missing.").** Every VeriBench Tiny-256 table and every full-896 table (paper, slides, repo notes, messages) carries at least one row with harness Pi and the best open-weight model we can run (currently Qwen3-14B in Pi 1.4.0, bf16, vLLM 0.11.0, 900 s per task, one attempt; settings in `paper_support/MODEL_SETTINGS_10-24-2026.md` of the veribench repo), scored under the same definitions, judge and denominator as the other rows, with harness and model as separate columns. Re-score saved outputs first; if outputs for the table's tasks are missing, run them on free hardware (empty GPUs, no paid API) rather than leave the row out. A cell not yet measured shows as unknown or a range, never zero. Pick the best open-weight model by the latest measured scores, not every candidate ("just the most likely ones to be the best always"). The same wording is in veribench `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`.

See [the exact format](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#compact-results-entry).

**Copy-ready collaborator message (Brando, 10-16-2026).** Whenever giving Brando research results, also include one **1–2 sentence message in Brando’s voice** that he can copy to Sanmi or the intended collaborator. Label it `Copy-ready message` outside the draft text. Use natural first-person wording where appropriate, scientific but easy to read; improve clarity without making his voice stiff or dense. Infer the audience from the conversation rather than always addressing Sanmi. State the main finding, enough scope and decisive numbers to interpret it, and the caveat or consequence that changes the takeaway. Distinguish measured results from hypotheses; preserve uncertainty and avoid causal overclaims.

Give one draft by default, not several alternatives. Keep internal paths, operational details, full statistical tables and chat-only closing blocks outside the copied message; relevant report links may accompany it. This message supplements the result summary and linked Markdown/Google reports, and is distinct from the opening weekly-update status sentence. It applies to research results, not routine administrative updates. Drafting does not authorize sending a message.

## Hard Rule 10

10. **Expand every acronym and define every piece of jargon on FIRST USE, in every response.** Applies to ordinary chat replies, not just to papers and reader-facing prose. The first time an abbreviation, initialism, or project-specific term appears in a response, write it out and say what it means in one short clause: `TBH (to be honest)`, `SCSC (Smooth Conjunctive Score for Code verification)`, `IC_pp (fraction of the agent's stated theorems it actually proved)`, `the fresh re-run` (rather than an in-house label like "Arm 2" that means nothing outside the experiment folder). Casual abbreviations count: `tbh`, `iirc`, `afaict`, `wrt`, `ETA`, `EOD`. So do metric symbols, factor names, experiment-internal vocabulary, file/label identifiers, and any term whose meaning depends on a document the reader is not currently looking at. Use the expansion once, then the short form freely for the rest of that response; re-expand in the next response, since Brando may be reading it on its own. **The trap this closes:** an agent reads an experiment README or a results summary, absorbs its private vocabulary, and then writes as if that vocabulary were shared -- but Brando is reading the reply, not the file the agent just read. **Why:** stated by Brando 2026-09-02 after a reply built an entire analysis on the in-house labels "Arm 1" / "Arm 2" without ever saying what they meant, leaving him to ask whether it meant the ARM hardware architecture. **Borrowed metaphors are jargon too:** "arm" there was the clinical-trial sense (one branch of an experiment), which is useless to a reader who is not running clinical trials -- the fix was not to define it but to rename it to what it actually was, a rescore of old runs versus a fresh re-run: "tell me what acronyms mean. I don't know what you're talking about" and "otherwise I don't know what the fuck you're talking about in your responses agents!" An unexplained acronym silently transfers the agent's work onto the reader. **Distinct from Trigger Rules 23 and 24**, which govern jargon in *reader-facing prose* (papers, blog posts); this Hard Rule governs every response the agent writes, to anyone, including Brando.

    **Codes carry a gloss (Brando, 10-13-2026).** In anything Brando reads (chat, weekly-update text, to-do lines, email), a code-like name may lead and may be bold, but on its first use in a message or section it is followed by a short parenthetical saying what it is, the way agent task titles do: `**V21-008** (the SampCert task, first candidate for the private V2.1 set)`, `**1A** (raters qualify on the first warm-up task only)`, `**T01** (Rylan)`, `**C17** (the amendment that fixed that rule)`. Later mentions in the same message may use the bare bold code; a plain-words name with the code in parentheses is equally fine. What is never fine is a bare code with no gloss anywhere in the message. Agent-to-agent records (checkpoints, ledgers, commit messages) may keep bare codes. **Why:** Brando, 10-13-2026, reading "102 set-N round: 1A, 2A, 3A ... V21-008 D1-D3 ... V008-01 D1-D4": "too many acronyms ... for me as a human it's difficult to read"; then, on an all-plain-language reply: "We can use both. The bolded acronym like names is nice. Maybe it just needs a parenthesis with a small description or something? Like the agent tasks titles sort of have."

## Hard Rule 11

11. **Show measured numbers alongside verdicts.** In every response or report, accompany pass/fail, accepted/rejected, threshold outcomes and qualitative judgments with the actual measured numerical results that support them; a verdict such as "none passed" alone hides how good the results are. Give clear metric names, units or scales, sample counts/denominators, the data split or phase, and uncertainty when available. For correlation analyses, report Pearson, Spearman and Kendall individually when available. When a score's value is itself interpreted (a level, threshold, "saturated" or a mapped scale), add one absolute-agreement statistic, such as ICC(A,1) or mean absolute error with mean bias, because correlations cannot show a constant offset; define bias with its sign every time, as the mean of (judge or model score minus the human or reference score), so a positive bias means the judge is lenient, and give the two means it comes from (Brando, 10-02-2026). Uncertainty, both always: give a 95% interval for every headline estimate, saying what was resampled (tasks, items, repeats) and what the interval does not cover, and add a p-value whenever a verdict is read from the number, against a named null (a zero difference, or the pre-declared threshold such as a 0.45 agreement gate or a 0.8 saturation line), naming the test; do not report p-values against "correlation is zero", which are uninformative, and write every interval as x [lo, hi] followed by p-val=Z naming the test, or p-val=n/a when no test was run (Brando, 10-02-2026). Full results reports follow the detailed example in [`workflows/statistics-reporting.md`](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#detailed-report-example-brando-10-02-2026): hypothesis as a question plus the metric, instrument with train/val/test agreement, results per system, a verdict bullet against the pre-declared threshold, a next step. For repeated scoring, report standard deviations and repetition counts, distinguishing variability across raw repeated scores from repeatability of aggregated scores (state what was aggregated and how). Compute these from data the experiment already has: this rule never requires extra runs, seeds, model calls or human labels, and a statistic the data cannot support is reported as "single run" or unavailable. Prefer cheap, honest reuse of that data to estimate uncertainty and variance, such as a bootstrap or permutation test over the independent unit (tasks or seeds, not correlated items within them) or statistics over repeats already made, and name the method. Validating a judge or proxy against human labels follows the [judge-human agreement checklist](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md#judge-human-agreement-checklist); both tiers, with reasons, are in [`workflows/statistics-reporting.md`](../workflows/statistics-reporting.md). "Raw numbers" means actual measured values, including useful summaries, not a dump of every observation. Mark missing metrics **unavailable** or **not measured**, never invent them. Show thresholds as secondary context and identify their source: user-chosen, protocol-defined or agent-suggested. A promising starting point is not an acceptance gate; this reporting rule never changes scientific protocols, results, thresholds or scoring. **Why:** Brando, 09-15-2026, asked to see the numbers behind judge-validation verdicts, not just whether they cleared a threshold. On 09-30-2026 a VeriBench judge with Pearson 0.86 still scored 0.18 above expert raters on average, which correlations alone could not show; Brando then asked that the rule stay cheap and general across training, reinforcement-learning and judge experiments.

**Presentation exception for compact result entries (10-15-2026).** Hard Rule 11 still governs the underlying evidence. In the 1–2 sentence format above, give the decisive values and denominator/scope, and put the full confidence intervals, resampling unit, p-value or `p-val=n/a`, mean bias, repeated-score variability and provenance in the two linked reports. Keep uncertainty in the short entry whenever omitting it would change the verdict. This is a brevity rule, not permission to imply an unmeasured result or unsupported generalization.

**Research precision: search before "unknown" (Brando, 10-24-2026).** Research and science have to be precise, and Brando should never need to remind an agent of this ("like we should never need a reminder like this ... Is research/science! it has to be precise man"; "I'd much rather you search the repo always to give me the accurate setting than saying idk"). Before any model setting (model ID, effort, thinking mode, checkpoint, quantization, serving engine and version, sampling settings, harness and its config), judge, definition, version, count or score goes into a table, caption, note or message, read it from the project's own records: the repo, experiment READMEs and protocols, run configs and launch scripts, receipts, saved run records and logs, the paper and its support files, `git log`/`git grep` including open pull requests, and the run's host when the record lives only there (fetch it; a setting that sits on a cluster is not unknown). Write `unknown` only after that search comes up empty, and have the caption name the paths searched; never write "idk", never guess, never ask Brando for something the repo could answer. Missing values stay unknown or a range, never zero. Every run records its settings in the project's GitHub experiment notes when it starts, so no later result says unknown because the setting sits on a cluster. Tables keep harness and model as separate columns. When two sources disagree, name the disagreement and use the primary one (the paper for definitions, saved run records for settings). Each project's `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` carries this rule near the top; VeriBench's full text is `docs/agent_rules/research_precision.md` in the veribench repo.

**Pi + best open-weight row in every VeriBench table (Brando, 10-24-2026: "can we always have at least 1 pi + best open source model we can run for this table? (or the full data set table too) Go run it if it's missing.").** Every VeriBench Tiny-256 table and every full-896 table (paper, slides, repo notes, messages) carries at least one row with harness Pi and the best open-weight model we can run (currently Qwen3-14B in Pi 1.4.0, bf16, vLLM 0.11.0, 900 s per task, one attempt; settings in `paper_support/MODEL_SETTINGS_10-24-2026.md` of the veribench repo), scored under the same definitions, judge and denominator as the other rows, with harness and model as separate columns. Re-score saved outputs first; if outputs for the table's tasks are missing, run them on free hardware (empty GPUs, no paid API) rather than leave the row out. A cell not yet measured shows as unknown or a range, never zero. Pick the best open-weight model by the latest measured scores, not every candidate ("just the most likely ones to be the best always"). The same wording is in veribench `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`.

## Trigger Rule 15

77. **Load `workflows/llm-judge-recipe.md` before building, selecting, validating or deploying any large language model (LLM) judge.** _Trigger: an LLM-as-a-judge metric, automatic grader, rubric scorer or reward model is being designed, tuned, validated, re-validated or applied to a new population of outputs, or its human labels are being collected; or a claim says a judge "agrees with humans" or "is validated"._ Read [`workflows/llm-judge-recipe.md`](../workflows/llm-judge-recipe.md), which applies Karpathy's "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" (2019) to judges. Before tuning: (1) hash-compare the exact judge inputs with what the human raters saw; (2) inspect the untuned judge's score distribution; (3) run a label-reproduction test (given the human label in its prompt, the judge must return it; an unconstrained fit on 2–3 items must succeed or be explained); (4) run controls with predicted values, plus human and dumb baselines. Then overfit the training split toward the human ceiling one change at a time, select on validation, test once with a receipt, report agreement in level as well as order (intraclass correlation ICC(A,1), absolute agreement, beside ICC(C,1), consistency), and re-validate on the population the judge will score. **Why:** VeriBench's formal-specification-coverage judge studies (experiments 75, 83, 92 and 92c) fed their judges a 09-03-2026 reference snapshot while the raters had rated April–May references; 9 of the 25 tasks' theorem statements differed. A one-line theorem-count baseline reached Spearman 0.543 with the references the raters saw, beating every one of those judges (0.17–0.28). Experiment 100's "overfit" step reached only 0.641 on training labels against a 0.794 human ceiling, and no one had tested whether the pipeline could reproduce labels at all (Karpathy: "If they do not, there is a bug somewhere and we cannot continue to the next stage.").

## Trigger Rule 82

82. **Every VeriBench experiment uses the current public VeriBench release, and says which one.** _Trigger: you plan, launch, score or report anything on VeriBench (the public set, `brando90/veribench`), or pin or update its task pack, scorer or splits._ As of 10-28-2026 the current public release is `veribench@1.3` (Harbor registry): 896 tasks in six splits (EasySet 41, CSSet 25, HumanEval 56, RealCodeSet 32, SecuritySet 460, IndustrySet 282) with the agent-spec v2 instruction; `veribench@1.0` to `@1.2` are superseded and only reproduce the NeurIPS-2026 numbers. `brando90/veribench` `main` was at `21846fd73b` that day. The authority is the `README.md` section "Public release and reproducibility" on `origin/main`, never your memory or an old pin. **Before each run:** run `git ls-remote https://github.com/brando90/veribench.git refs/heads/main` and read that README section; if the release, task count or splits differ from the above, use the new one and update this rule and the project's pin in the same reviewed commit. A new protocol uses the current release; a locked protocol keeps its recorded pins, which you name. Name the version beside every VeriBench number (VBV1 is the public set; the private VBV2 and `vb-priv-bmg` sets are separate). **Why:** Brando, 10-28-2026: "we also need an agent's config file, ClaudeMD file, so that we are always using the state-of-the-art VeriBench public for this."

## Trigger Rule 83

83. **High-uncertainty work (research, startup): ask first whether the thing should exist, test it fast, then push velocity.** _Trigger: a research, experiment, eval or startup request where the outcome or the need for the thing is unknown._ Agents bias toward building something big and complicated before anyone knows it should exist. Instead: **(1)** name the highest-risk question; **(2)** run the quickest test that de-risks it, on the machine you are already on, with the harness at hand (Pi or Claude Code; a state-of-the-art harness named approximately is enough); **(3)** email Brando the results and write them into the repo's MD files (vb-priv, vb-priv-bmg). Build endpoints, queues and cross-machine paths in parallel, as second priority. **Trade-off:** the highest-risk direction is not the only thing that matters; velocity does too. Once the test obviously covers the main risk, optimize velocity aggressively. This refines Rule 50 and waives none of its limits (correctness, safety, budgets, permissions); GPU jobs still follow Rules 55 and 80. Logins follow the "Login checks and machine access" section of each project's `AGENTS.md`. Background he named: Stanford Lean LaunchPad, *The Lean Startup*, Michael Bernstein's CS197. **Why:** Brando, 10-29-2026, after the frontier evals on the private VeriBench set were held up by queues, logins and endpoint building: why are you overcomplicating this; his agents should have had these de-risking rules. Credit: cc opus 5.5 xhigh.

## Trigger Rule 84

84. **vb-priv: int_ref is the most important metric; run it first and lead every update with it.** _Trigger: you run, score or report anything on vb-priv or vb-priv-bmg (also VeriBench, VeriBench DT, cert/search judge for new runs)._ Run the internal + reference evaluation (int_ref) once, save every per-task result, and derive int from those saved scores instead of running int separately (int_ref is a superset of int). Lead each update with harsh int_ref, then smooth int_ref, then int; if int_ref was not computed, say so and why. **Why:** Brando, 10-29-2026: "we should be doing int_ref as the most important metric." and "int_ref is a super set of int, shouldn't we be computing int_ref and then from that we compute int?" Credit: cc opus 5.5 xhigh.

# llm-judge-recipe.md — Karpathy's recipe for building and validating an LLM judge

**TLDR:** Build an LLM judge (automatic grader, rubric scorer, reward model) the way Karpathy trains a neural net. Become one with the human labels, then earn trust in the end-to-end pipeline through sanity checks *before* tuning: a byte-level input audit, the untuned judge's score distribution, a label-reproduction test, controls, and human and dumb baselines. ### 1. Become one with the human labels (before writing any judge prompt)

Karpathy: "The first step to training a neural net is to not touch any neural net code at all and instead begin by thoroughly inspecting your data."

- Histogram the labels. Find degenerate items (for example references with nothing to cover, where every candidate deserves full marks), duplicates, and items whose inputs changed during rating.
- Compute rater agreement and the **human ceiling** per split: one rater held out against the others, Karpathy's "annotate the test data twice and for each example treat one annotation as prediction and the second as ground truth". That ceiling is the achievable bar, not 1.0.
- Study how the raters disagree, and choose the target deliberately.

**VeriBench:**
- 15 of the 75 items (5 tasks) had `True`-only placeholder references.
- Experts rated bundled correctness theorems 1–3 where lenient raters gave 4–5.
- The human ceilings were 0.794 / 0.899 / 0.733 on train / validation / test.

All of this was established systematically only in experiment 100, after four earlier judge studies.

### 2. Build the end-to-end skeleton and earn trust in it with sanity checks

Karpathy: "set up a full training + evaluation skeleton and gain trust in its correctness via a series of experiments."

**2.1 "Visualize just before the net" → a byte-level input audit.** Karpathy: "visualize exactly what goes into your network … This is the only 'source of truth'." Dump the exact rendered judge prompt for several items, and hash-compare every embedded file (source, reference, candidate) with what the raters saw.
- **VeriBench skipped this for weeks.** Experiments 75, 83, 92 and 92c fed their judges a 09-03-2026 reference snapshot, while the raters had rated against April–May references. Nine of the 25 tasks' theorem statements differed, and five had been placeholders at rating time.
- Re-analyzing one saved judge (R4, Sonnet 5) split by whether its reference matched gives Spearman 0.469 on matched items and 0.095 on mismatched ones. One diff would have saved the studies.

**2.2 "Verify loss @ init" → the untuned judge's score distribution.** Before any tuning, run the plain judge and look at its histogram, entropy, modal share and a handful of rationales.
- **VeriBench:** the NeurIPS-era coverage judge put 85–87% of task scores at exactly 0.1. Replaying its loose parser on 1,185 logged responses mapped 94.3% of them to 0.1. A histogram shows this in seconds.

**2.3 "Overfit one batch" → a label-reproduction test.** Karpathy: "Overfit a single batch of only a few examples … verify that we can reach the lowest achievable loss (e.g. zero) … If they do not, there is a bug somewhere and we cannot continue to the next stage." Two judge versions:
- **Label in the prompt.** Give the judge each item's expert score, and optionally the rationale, and ask it to return that score. Agreement must be about 1.0. Anything less is a pipeline bug: parsing, scale mapping, item–label misalignment, truncation.
- **Unconstrained fit on 2–3 items.** Iterate the prompt freely, item-specific hints allowed, until the judge matches the experts on those items. If it can't, inspect the item. You will find either a label–input mismatch (the rater saw different files) or a construct the prompt cannot express. In VeriBench this would have exposed the reference mismatch on the first affected item.
- **VeriBench never ran either test.** Its "overfit" gate was training Spearman ≥ 0.60, a bar to clear rather than a reproduction test.

**2.4 "Input-independent baseline" → controls with predicted values.** Karpathy: "This should perform worse than when you actually plug in your data without zeroing it out."
- Blank candidate, vacuous claim and a shuffled candidate from another task should score about 0. The oracle (reference judged against itself) should score about the maximum. A minimal reference should score partially.
- Write the expected values down first, and check the controls themselves. VeriBench's "half-deleted reference" control was mis-specified: a redundant reference keeps full coverage, so the judge was logically right. It was replaced prospectively.

**2.5 "Human baseline."** Karpathy: "Whenever possible evaluate your own (human) accuracy and compare to it." Use the leave-one-rater-out ceiling from step 1. "Human level" means matching that ceiling.

**2.6 Dumb baselines.** Length, theorem count, placeholder count, always predicting the mean. The judge must beat them on the non-degenerate items. If a dumb baseline beats your judge, stop and find out why before tuning anything.
- **VeriBench:** a one-line baseline, min(1, candidate theorems ÷ reference theorems), reaches Spearman 0.543 on the full 75-item pool with the references the raters saw. That beats every earlier LLM judge (0.17–0.28). Fed the 09-03 snapshot the earlier judges used, the same baseline falls to 0.273. It would have exposed both the weak judges and the reference mismatch at zero cost.

**2.7 "Fix random seed" → repeat stability.** LLM judges are stochastic. Run k ≥ 3 repeats, report per-item repeat SD and test–retest ICC, and pin model IDs, configurations and prompt fingerprints by hash. VeriBench's selected judge has repeat SD 0.02.

**2.8 "Add significant digits to your eval."**
- Report task-bootstrap intervals, on all items and on the non-degenerate items separately.
- Use several agreement statistics: Spearman, Kendall, Pearson, plus ICC(A,1), which penalizes level, beside ICC(C,1), which does not.
- Never rely on a single small split alone.

**2.9 "Generalize a special case."** Get one task's items right end to end before running the whole pool.

- **Read the worst training items after every iteration.** The plain human-mirror judge ordered candidates *within* a task opposite to the experts (within-task correlation −0.38 on training); the conventions fixed it.
- **Expect training agreement near the human ceiling.** If it stays well below, stop and investigate before moving on. Karpathy: "if we are not able to reach a low error rate with any model at all that may again indicate some issues, bugs, or misconfiguration."

> **Why wasn't VeriBench's training agreement close to 1.0?** The selected ensemble reached 0.641 on train against a human ceiling of 0.794.
> 1. **Almost no capacity to memorize.** Training labels entered the judge only as four written conventions and four rated examples. An item's own label never appears in its prompt, because the examples are leave-task-out. A prompt-level judge is closer to a fixed model with a few hints than to a network fit to its labels. "Overfitting" in Karpathy's sense, driving training error to zero, was never attempted; the gate was a bar at 0.60.
> 2. **Noisy labels.** The target is a three-expert mean on a 0–5 scale, and one expert agrees with the other two at 0.794 on train. A judge of true coverage cannot correlate perfectly with a noisy mean.
> 3. **Label–input mismatches on training items.** Five tasks' references changed while raters were rating, so the judge may have scored different bytes than the raters saw. Convention 2 ("restating the code earns 0–1") also misfired on one placeholder item the experts rated 5/5 (`5_unsafeFormatString_safe__agent2`). > 4. **Coarse outputs.** Integer scores, the median of 3 per member averaged across two members, produce many ties, which cap rank correlations.
> 5. **Small splits.** Random 10/5/10 re-splits of the 25 tasks produce a train–test gap at least this large 18.9% of the time; a 10-task Spearman has SD about 0.12.
>
> The label-reproduction test (2.3) separates reasons 1–2 (capacity and noise, acceptable) from bugs (not acceptable). Run it, and "why isn't train 100%?" has a measured answer instead of a guess.

- **"Get more data."** Karpathy: "the by far best and preferred way to regularize a model in any practical setting is to add more real training data." For judges that means more human ratings.
- **When ratings are scarce, cross-validate the whole recipe.** Rebuild the judge in each fold from the other folds' labels, including rules written automatically from those folds' errors, and score the held-out fold. It also showed how little the tuning bought: the raters'-instructions judge with no tuning was within 0.002 (Claude Opus 5.5) to 0.087 (GPT-6 Sol) of the recipe, both intervals including zero. - **VeriBench:** test Spearman 0.826 [0.32, 0.97], Kendall 0.698, Pearson 0.858, ICC(A,1) 0.727 against a ceiling of 0.733, which passed the prespecified gate. - **Check level, not only order.** High correlation can coexist with leniency.

  - If you fit a monotone score mapping to the experts' scale, label it as a separately fitted procedure, evaluated on held-out ratings.
- **Controls travel with the judge.** Re-run them on every new population.
- **Re-audit inputs whenever references change.** Any edit after rating breaks the judge–rater correspondence, so version the references and re-check hashes.
