- **"Don't be a hero."** Start from the raters' own instructions (a human-mirror judge), not an invented rubric. In VeriBench's held-out ablations, matched inputs and the rater-derived conventions carried most of the gain.
- **"Complexify only one at a time,"** with a changelog line per change. VeriBench went H0 human mirror (training Spearman 0.460) → H1, adding four conventions written from training disagreements (0.562) → H2, adding four leave-task-out rated examples (0.591) → H2 on Claude Opus 5.5 max (0.663).
- **Read the worst training items after every iteration.** The plain human-mirror judge ordered candidates *within* a task opposite to the experts (within-task correlation −0.38 on training); the conventions fixed it.
- **Expect training agreement near the human ceiling.** If it stays well below, stop and investigate before moving on. Karpathy: "if we are not able to reach a low error rate with any model at all that may again indicate some issues, bugs, or misconfiguration."

> **Why wasn't VeriBench's training agreement close to 1.0?** The selected ensemble reached 0.641 on train against a human ceiling of 0.794.
> 1. **Almost no capacity to memorize.** Training labels entered the judge only as four written conventions and four rated examples. An item's own label never appears in its prompt, because the examples are leave-task-out. A prompt-level judge is closer to a fixed model with a few hints than to a network fit to its labels. "Overfitting" in Karpathy's sense, driving training error to zero, was never attempted; the gate was a bar at 0.60.
> 2. **Noisy labels.** The target is a three-expert mean on a 0–5 scale, and one expert agrees with the other two at 0.794 on train. A judge of true coverage cannot correlate perfectly with a noisy mean.
> 3. **Label–input mismatches on training items.** Five tasks' references changed while raters were rating, so the judge may have scored different bytes than the raters saw. Convention 2 ("restating the code earns 0–1") also misfired on one placeholder item the experts rated 5/5 (`5_unsafeFormatString_safe__agent2`). Without that item and those tasks, train reaches 0.891 (validation 0.883, test 0.885). That is a post-hoc diagnostic, not a claim.
> 4. **Coarse outputs.** Integer scores, the median of 3 per member averaged across two members, produce many ties, which cap rank correlations.
> 5. **Small splits.** Random 10/5/10 re-splits of the 25 tasks produce a train–test gap at least this large 18.9% of the time; a 10-task Spearman has SD about 0.12.
>
> The label-reproduction test (2.3) separates reasons 1–2 (capacity and noise, acceptable) from bugs (not acceptable). Run it, and "why isn't train 100%?" has a measured answer instead of a guess.

### 4. Regularize and generalize

- Keep rules general and rated examples leave-task-out. Select among at most three frozen finalists, on validation only.
- **"Get more data."** Karpathy: "the by far best and preferred way to regularize a model in any practical setting is to add more real training data." For judges that means more human ratings.
- **When ratings are scarce, cross-validate the whole recipe.** Rebuild the judge in each fold from the other folds' labels, including rules written automatically from those folds' errors, and score the held-out fold. Every rating then becomes evaluation data exactly once; this is VeriBench experiment 104.
- **Expect the honest number to be lower, and report it.** VeriBench's cross-validated recipe scored Spearman 0.602 [0.286, 0.834] and ICC(A,1) 0.593 over all 75 items. That is below the frozen judge's 0.826 on its 30-item test and 0.756 on the whole pool, of which 30 items had shaped its rules. It also showed how little the tuning bought: the raters'-instructions judge with no tuning was within 0.002 (Claude Opus 5.5) to 0.087 (GPT-6 Sol) of the recipe, both intervals including zero. The five 15-item folds ranged from 0.35 to 0.86, another reminder that one small split is a noisy estimate.
- You cannot relabel already-used ratings as a "test set" for a judge designed after reading them.

### 5. Test once, with a receipt

- Freeze the judge by hash before any test call, run the test once, and write a receipt.
- Report every agreement statistic with intervals, the non-degenerate items separately, and the human ceiling. Disclose earlier looks at the same test labels.
- **VeriBench:** test Spearman 0.826 [0.32, 0.97], Kendall 0.698, Pearson 0.858, ICC(A,1) 0.727 against a ceiling of 0.733, which passed the prespecified gate. On the 24 ordinary test items the Spearman is 0.652 [−0.17, 0.92]: placeholder items carried part of the pass, and 8 ordinary tasks cannot establish rank agreement on their own.

### 6. Squeeze out the juice

Karpathy: "Model ensembles are a pretty much guaranteed way to gain 2% of accuracy on anything." For judges, average members from different model families. That adds accuracy and dilutes self-preference, such as a Claude judge scoring Claude agents. VeriBench uses GPT-6 Sol high plus Claude Opus 5.5 max, the mean of the two members' medians.

### 7. Apply carefully, and re-validate on the new distribution

- **Transfer is an assumption.** A judge validated on one population of outputs (VeriBench: 05-2026 Claude 3.7 Sonnet candidates) is unvalidated on another (frontier agents). Re-validate with fresh human ratings drawn from the population it will score. Spend them mostly on evaluation: the judge needs few labels to build.
- **Check level, not only order.** High correlation can coexist with leniency.
  - VeriBench's judge effectively uses three levels (about 0.1, 0.8 and 1.0). Items the experts rated as partial coverage (0.3–0.6, mean 0.44) came out at about 0.78.
  - Report ICC(A,1) beside ICC(C,1), and a band table (expert band → judge mean).
  - If you fit a monotone score mapping to the experts' scale, label it as a separately fitted procedure, evaluated on held-out ratings.
- **Controls travel with the judge.** Re-run them on every new population.
- **Re-audit inputs whenever references change.** Any edit after rating breaks the judge–rater correspondence, so version the references and re-check hashes.

## What skipping the sanity checks cost: the VeriBench timeline

| When (2026) | Study | Outcome | Skipped check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 04–05 | NeurIPS coverage judge (Sonnet 4.6, symmetric equivalence rubric) | 85–87% of task scores at 0.1; published without validation | 2.2 score distribution; parser trace |
| 09-03 to 09-12 | Experiment 75 judge search, locked 10/5/10 split | No winner; finalist test Spearman 0.271 | 2.1 byte-level input audit (judges saw 09-03 references) |
| 09 | Experiments 83, 92, 92c (frontier directional judges, open-weight and Gemini judges) | All below the 0.45 gate; best expert Spearman 0.17–0.28 on the full pool | 2.1 again; 2.6 (a theorem-count ratio scored 0.543) |
| 09-28 | Experiment 100 Phase 0, zero calls | Found the mismatch; with matched inputs a judge passed a held-out test | — |
| 09-28 | Experiment 100 "overfit" step | Training 0.641, below the human ceiling; explained only by a later audit | 2.3 label-reproduction test |

## Checklist (paste into a judge study's protocol)

- [ ] Labels read; degenerate items flagged; human ceiling per split computed; target chosen deliberately.
- [ ] The exact judge inputs hash-match what the raters saw, for every item.

 # Trustworthy theorem judges
 
-Can a language model tell which gold-reference theorems follow from an agent’s formal specification? We collect independent human ratings of statement coverage. The planned judge comparison uses the same candidates and gold statements twice, with and without the gold proofs. A separate comparison asks how the judgments relate to what a theorem prover can establish.
+**Doc link:** <https://github.com/brando90/trustworthy-theorem-judges/blob/main/README.md>
+
+**TLDR:** This project studies artificial-intelligence (AI), agent, and large language model (LLM) judges for formal specification coverage (FSC). It contains a prospective human-rating methodology, historical VeriBench judge evidence, and an AAAI-27 workshop paper draft; fresh validation results are pending human data.
+
+Given original Python source, a candidate Lean formalization, and a gold reference, can a judge predict how qualified humans rate the candidate's coverage of the required specifications? A gold statement may follow from several candidate statements together. Proof correctness and statement coverage are different properties.
+
+## Project boundary
+
+This repository owns the AI/agent/LLM judge study. VeriBench's intended evaluation direction is a **prover judge**: AI may guide proof search, while the prover checks whether the required implication has been established. A search timeout is unresolved, not evidence of non-entailment. This documentation records that project boundary; it does not change VeriBench's scorer or relabel its historical LLM-based results.
+
+## Methodology and paper
+
+- [Study methodology and collection design](experiments/02_probabilistic_ordinal_judge/README.md): predict the six-category conditional human-rating distribution with the ranked probability score as the primary loss; correlations are secondary diagnostics.
+- [Historical results and provenance](experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/README.md): preserved aggregate receipts, limitations, and a clear separation from new validation.
+- [AAAI-27 workshop paper](paper_latex/AAAI_2027_Evaluation_AI_Scientists/README.md): anonymous LaTeX source and compiled PDF using the official author kit.
+- [Experiment index](experiments/README.md): status, scope, and next evidence needed.
+
+The starting collection design has **896 tasks, four solver configurations, and 24 distinct raters** (eight for training/validation and 16 for the final audit). Collect three ratings per artifact and eight total on a 128-task audit subset. Separate training/validation artifacts from fresh final-audit outputs: **14,848 individual ratings** in total. These are planning counts, not a precision guarantee or a completed collection. The pilot must establish feasibility, thresholds, and uncertainty before the test is opened.
+
+## Verify and build
+
+```sh
+python3 experiments/02_probabilistic_ordinal_judge/scripts/validate_design.py
+python3 scripts/check_project.py
+python3 scripts/build_paper.py
+git diff --check
+```
+
+The paper build requires a TeX installation with `latexmk` and the packages required by the official AAAI-27 style. It builds in a temporary directory and writes the current PDF beside its source.

    79	3. **Previously seen ratings.** The receipt discloses earlier exposure by experiments 75 and 83 and a descriptive initial audit. “One-shot test” refers to the selected candidate's test invocation, not a pristine dataset. The exact total number of judge versions that previously saw these ratings and the resulting selection inflation are not established by the imported receipt, explainer, or continued-paper appendix; no numerical inflation estimate is asserted.
    80	4. **Single solver distribution.** Repeated samples from one older solver do not test transfer across agent families, tools, current model versions, or larger projects.
    81	5. **Absolute score bias.** Correlation does not remove the positive mean bias or establish itemwise agreement.
    82	6. **Human and judge repeat limits.** Two or three expert ratings per file and three paired-model passes provide limited evidence about conditional rating distributions and full-judge repeatability.
    83	
    84	These limitations motivate fresh task/agent/rater splits and distribution-sensitive metrics in the new methodology.
    85	They are not problems that disappear merely by adding more correlated ratings to the same historical items.
    86	
    87	## Original paper versus later recipe
    88	
    89	The original **Pearson 0.703349** row uses a separate `gpt-5.3-codex` human-rubric judge with an isotonic score mapping fit on each training fold and evaluated on the disjoint validation fold.
    90	Its raw zero-shot Pearson value is **0.515424** on the same archived 72-item target.
    91	Judge and mapping choices used that validation protocol; there is no independent test-set counterpart.
    92	The source paper reports that the raw scorer package is unavailable, so this archive preserves the aggregate record rather than claiming a complete executable reproduction.
    93	
    94	Experiment 104 evaluates an **automated recipe**, with fold-specific model-written conventions and examples and five calls per member, rather than the frozen experiment 100 judge.
    95	Its original raw-float aggregate gives Spearman **0.601533 [0.285578, 0.834392]**, usually written **0.602**.
    96	The published addendum rounds predictions before ranking to preserve mathematical ties and reports **0.603 [0.287, 0.836]**; use that figure when citing the continued paper.
    97	The original excerpt is retained as provenance and must not silently overwrite the corrected figure.
    98	The same addendum changes the second-repetition Spearman from **0.654** to **0.660**.
    99	Its original two-repetition mean is not relabeled as a tie-corrected result.

     1	# Probabilistic ordinal judges of formal specification coverage
     2	
     3	**Doc link:** <https://github.com/brando90/trustworthy-theorem-judges/blob/main/experiments/02_probabilistic_ordinal_judge/README.md>
     4	
     5	**TLDR:** Predict the conditional distribution of expert ratings with a six-category probability forecast, select the judge by ranked probability score, and evaluate fresh outputs with separate task, agent, and human holdouts.
     6

     8	
     9	This repository studies artificial intelligence (AI), agent, and large language model (LLM) judges of formal specification coverage (FSC). VeriBench's separate direction is a prover judge, with AI guiding proof search; this study does not implement that migration or report new prover results. Historical scalar LLM-judge evidence is a baseline, not evidence that the new probabilistic judge works.
    10

    12	
    13	## Target and measurement
    14	
    15	For each candidate artifact, use the same triple for humans and the judge:
    16	
    17	\[
    18	z=(x_{\mathrm{input}},y_{\mathrm{pred}},y^*),
    19	\qquad r\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.
    20	\]
    21	
    22	Here, the inputs are the Python source, candidate Lean output, and gold Lean reference. FSC concerns coverage of the required formal specifications, meaning theorem statements without their proofs; proof completion is a separate property. A reference can be incomplete or wrong, so agreement with reference-assisted humans is not itself a proof of semantic correctness.
    23	
    24	Define the human target as the probability mass function
    25	
    26	\[
    27	p^*(r\mid z)=\Pr(\text{a qualified expert assigns }r\text{ to }z)
    28	\]
    29	
    30	under the specified rubric and expert sampling population. The judge returns six nonnegative probabilities \(q_\theta(r\mid z)\) that sum to one. Its expected normalized score is \(\sum_{r=0}^5 r q_\theta(r\mid z)/5\). Preserve the probability vector and each individual human rating; do not reduce disagreements to one consensus rating.
    31	
    32	The target is agreement **conditional on the same artifact**, then averaged across artifacts. Pooled rating histograms can match perfectly while the judge swaps every high and low rating. Repeated stochastic scalar outputs from an LLM are not automatically predictions of human disagreement. This six-probability output is a new experimental condition.
    33	
    34	## Primary objective
    35	
    36	For \(Q_c=\sum_{r=0}^c q_r\), use the normalized ranked probability score (RPS):
    37	
    38	\[
    39	S(q,r)=\frac15\sum_{c=0}^4\left(Q_c-\mathbf1\{r\le c\}\right)^2\in[0,1].
    40	\]
    41	
    42	Let \(P_c\) be the true cumulative human probabilities. Then
    43	
    44	\[
    45	\mathbb E_{R\sim p^*}S(q,R)
    46	=\underbrace{\frac15\sum_c(Q_c-P_c)^2}_{\text{conditional distribution error}}
    47	+\underbrace{\frac15\sum_cP_c(1-P_c)}_{\text{human disagreement}}.
    48	\]
    49	
    50	Thus, minimizing expected RPS targets the entire conditional rating distribution; its unrestricted optimum is \(q=p^*\). On the normalized rating scale, the Wasserstein distance is \(W_1(q,p^*)=\frac15\sum_c|Q_c-P_c|\), and \(W_1^2\) is at most the excess expected RPS. This justifies the objective, not a claim that any chosen judge achieves it. Proper scoring rules are established methodology ([Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf)).
    51	
    52	For artifact \(i\) with \(m_i\) assigned people, optimize
    53	
    54	\[
    55	\widehat L(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{m_i}\sum_h S(q_\theta(z_i),r_{ih}).
    56	\]
    57	
    58	Average ratings **within each artifact first**, then average artifacts equally. The dense subset must not gain extra weight merely because more people rate it. Pin model version, harness, tools, effort, prompt, budget, generation seed policy, and failure policy before generating outputs. They are four deliberately selected systems, not four independent random draws from a population of all agents.

    84

Measure minutes per review and fatigue effects during the pilot. The dense subset supplies better distribution diagnostics; eight ratings do not reveal the exact population distribution for an artifact.
    86	
    87	## Identity splits and assignment
    88	
    89	1. Group related task identities before splitting. In particular, related security variants stay together; never split individual rating rows or near-duplicate artifacts across training, validation, and test. Preserve exact 64/64/768 counts only if grouping permits them; otherwise amend the design and recompute its budget before inspection of test results.
    90	2. Recruit the 8 training/validation experts and 16 final-audit experts as disjoint pools from the declared qualified population. Record qualifications, recruitment frame, exclusions, and nonresponse privately. The final-audit people supply no ratings for judge selection.

    94

    96

    98	
    99	Fit candidate judges on the 64 training tasks, then select using artifact-weighted mean validation RPS on the 64 validation tasks. Record every candidate, prompt iteration, input choice, and score-mapping fit. Human-group cross-validation within the eight training/validation people may guide selection; it does not replace the separate audit pool. Repeatedly inspected validation results are selection evidence, not independent test evidence ([Cawley and Talbot, 2010](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)).
   100

   102	
   103	- **Main judge:** train and select using all four agents' training/validation outputs.
   104	- **Four leave-one-agent-out judges:** for each target agent, train and select using only the other three agents' outputs. Exclude target-agent outputs and ratings from both training and validation, including prompt examples and human rationales used to construct that fit. Evaluate on the target agent's 768 held-out tasks with final-audit people.
   105

This tests whether the **judge training/selection procedure** transfers to each excluded configuration. It does not establish that the main judge trained on all four generalizes to every future agent. Record prior experiment and pretraining exposure; a leave-one-agent-out split cannot erase historical exposure to that model family.
   107	
   108	Before opening final ratings, fix judge versions, analysis code, endpoints, treatment of failed/missing calls, all thresholds, and the number of repeats. Evaluate the final test once. Later changes are new conditions requiring fresh test evidence for clean claims.
   109	
   110	## Analysis and criteria
   111	
   112	Report artifact-weighted mean RPS and paired differences against: (1) a constant human-rating distribution estimated on training ratings, (2) a fixed rubric/reference-assisted judge, (3) a correlation-selected judge, and (4) the RPS-selected judge. Use matched artifacts and record unequal model-call budgets.    133	
   134	| Controlled edit | Expected FSC response |
   135	|---|---|
   136	| Remove a necessary specification obligation | Lower coverage |
   137	| Narrow a precondition to exclude required inputs | Lower coverage of the required domain |
   138	| Use a semantically equivalent specification | Similar coverage |

1	**Yes—your goal is now a coherent statistical learning problem: predict the distribution of ratings that qualified humans would assign to the same submission, then test whether that prediction transfers to new tasks, agents, and people.**
     2	
     3	That is a stronger and more useful goal than maximizing correlation. It also changes my earlier data recommendation: **five fixed humans can define a reference panel, but they do not establish generalization to new experts.** For that broader goal, I would recruit more distinct humans and ask each to rate fewer files.
     4	
     5	I’ll address your three questions directly, then give one concrete starting design.
     6	
     7	## 1. Why is this approach mathematically justified?
     8	
     9	### The crucial distinction: match distributions conditional on the submission
    10	
    11	Keep your notation:
    12	
    13	\[
    14	z=(x_{\mathrm{input}},y_{\mathrm{pred}},y^*).
    15	\]
    16	
    17	Define
    18	
    19	\[
    20	p^*(r\mid z)
    21	=
    22	\Pr(\text{a qualified expert assigns rating }r\text{ to }z),
    23	\]
    24	
    25	under a specified rubric and expert population. Your judge predicts
    26	
    27	\[
    28	q_\theta(r\mid z),\qquad r\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.
    29	\]
    30	
    31	Your objective is to make these distributions close **for the same \(z\)**, averaged over the submissions you care about.
    32	
    33	This qualification matters even if you compare every moment or use KL divergence. Consider:
    34	
    35	| Submission group | Human rating | AI rating |
    36	|---|---:|---:|
    37	| Half the submissions | 0 | 5 |
    38	| Other half | 5 | 0 |
    39	
    40	The pooled AI and human distributions are identical. Their means, variances, skewness, kurtosis, and every other moment match. Pooled KL divergence is zero.
    41	
    42	**Yet every AI judgment is wrong.**
    43	
    44	Therefore, the target should be
    45	
    46	\[
    47	\boxed{
    48	\mathcal D(\theta)
    49	=
    50	\mathbb E_z\!\left[
    51	D\!\left(p^*(\cdot\mid z),q_\theta(\cdot\mid z)\right)
    52	\right].
    53	}
    54	\]
    55	
    56	Compare the distributions **within each submission**, then average. Do not pool all ratings before comparing.
    57	
    58	A scatterplot of AI mean versus human mean remains useful, especially with the identity line \(y=x\), but it discards disagreement around those means. More sophisticated dependence measures do not solve this automatically: a judge can depend strongly on human scores while consistently reversing or distorting them.
    59	
    60	### Yes, this really is probabilistic classification
    61	
    62	Your “we could even do classification” observation is correct. There are six possible rating categories, so the judge can output six probabilities:
    63	
    64	\[
    65	q_\theta(z)=(q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4,q_5),
    66	\qquad
    67	\sum_{k=0}^{5}q_k=1.
    68	\]
    69	
    70	The categories are ordered, making this **probabilistic ordinal prediction**.
    71	
    72	The intended interpretation is “the probabilities of different human ratings.” Repeated stochastic LLM scores do not automatically have that interpretation; those probabilities themselves must be learned or calibrated against human data.
    73	
    74	### KL is justified—but I prefer an ordinal proper loss here
    75	
    76	Forward KL is a principled choice because
    77	
    78	\[
    79	\mathbb E_{R\sim p^*}[-\log q_\theta(R\mid z)]
    80	=
    81	\underbrace{\mathsf H(p^*(\cdot\mid z))}_{\text{independent of }\theta}
    82	+
    83	D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^*\|q_\theta).
    84	\]
    85	
    86	Thus, minimizing expected cross-entropy minimizes forward KL. You can train using individual human ratings without first knowing the complete human distribution.
    87	
    88	However, ordinary cross-entropy does not use the ordering of the categories, and it becomes infinite if the judge assigns zero probability to an observed rating. Proper scoring rules offer alternatives that target the full distribution. [sites.stat.washington.edu](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
    89	
    90	**My recommendation is the normalized ranked probability score, or RPS.** This is the discrete version of the CRPS we discussed, specialized to your six ordered categories.
    91	
    92	Define cumulative probabilities
    93	
    94	\[
    95	Q_c=\sum_{k=0}^{c}q_k,
    96	\qquad c=0,\ldots,4.
    97	\]
    98	
    99	Then, for an observed human rating \(r\),
   100	
   101	\[
   102	\boxed{
   103	S_{\mathrm{RPS}}(q,r)
   104	=
   105	\frac15\sum_{c=0}^{4}
   106	\left(Q_c-\mathbf1\{r\le c\}\right)^2.
   107	}
   108	\]
   109	
   110	This loss lies in \([0,1]\). It scores the predicted probabilities of all five threshold events: rating at most 0, at most 1, and so on. Using cumulative probabilities is what makes it sensitive to the ordering. [sites.stat.washington.edu](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
   111	
   112	### The equation that justifies the objective
   113	
   114	Let \(P_c\) be the corresponding cumulative human probabilities. Expanding the squares gives
   115	
   116	\[
   117	\boxed{
   118	\mathbb E_{R\sim p^*}S_{\mathrm{RPS}}(q,R)
   119	=
   120	\underbrace{\frac15\sum_{c=0}^{4}(Q_c-P_c)^2}
   121	_{\text{distributional prediction error}}
   122	+
   123	\underbrace{\frac15\sum_{c=0}^{4}P_c(1-P_c)}
   124	_{\text{human disagreement}}.
   125	}
   126	\]
   127	
   128	The second term does not depend on your judge. Therefore, minimizing expected RPS minimizes the first term, whose unrestricted optimum is exactly
   129	
   130	\[
   131	q(\cdot\mid z)=p^*(\cdot\mid z).
   132	\]
   133	
   134	That answers your first question: **the population optimization objective has precisely the distribution you want as its optimum.**
   135	
   136	There is also a connection to an interpretable distance. For ratings normalized by dividing by 5,
   137	
   138	\[
   139	W_1(q,p^*)=\frac15\sum_{c=0}^{4}|Q_c-P_c|.
   140	\]
   141	
   142	By Cauchy–Schwarz,
   143	
   144	\[
   145	\boxed{
   146	W_1(q,p^*)^2
   147	\le
   148	\underbrace{
   149	\mathbb E_{p^*}S_{\mathrm{RPS}}(q,R)
   150	-
   151	\mathbb E_{p^*}S_{\mathrm{RPS}}(p^*,R)
   152	}_{\text{excess RPS}}.
   153	}
   154	\]
   155	
   156	So reducing excess RPS controls a distance between the complete conditional rating distributions.
   157	
   158	**This establishes that the objective is appropriate. It does not establish that a particular model, prompt optimizer, or dataset will achieve low error.** That is what the evaluation must determine.
   159	
   160	### What about matching all moments?
   161	
   162	With six known possible values, normalization plus the first five raw moments identifies the distribution in principle. But learning six probabilities—or five cumulative probabilities—is more direct.
   163	
   164	Mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis alone generally do not identify a six-category distribution. More importantly, even matching every moment must happen conditionally on the submission. The reversed-grades example defeats pooled moment matching.
   165	
   166	### The practical training objective
   167	
   168	For artifact \(i\), let \(H_i\) be its assigned raters and \(m_i=|H_i|\). Optimize
   169	
   170	\[
   171	\hat\theta
   172	=
   173	\arg\min_\theta
   174	\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}
   175	\frac1{m_i}\sum_{h\in H_i}
   176	S_{\mathrm{RPS}}\!\left(q_\theta(\cdot\mid z_i),r_{ih}\right).
   177	\]
   178	
   179	Average within each artifact first, then across artifacts. This prevents heavily annotated artifacts from automatically dominating.
   180	
   181	Randomly assigned individual ratings can estimate this objective. **You do not need an accurately reconstructed human histogram for every training artifact before learning**, just as probabilistic classification does not require knowing the true class probabilities for every training example.
   182	
   183	## 2. How do we justify \(T,A,H\), and generalization across them?
   184	
   185	Your idea of holding out fractions of all three dimensions is right, with two conditions:
   186	
   187	1. Hold out **identities**, not merely individual tensor cells.
   188	2. State which population those held-out identities represent.
   189	
   190	For humans, I would define the population as something like:
   191	
   192	> Qualified Lean/formal-methods reviewers who receive the specified task information, reference, and grading instructions.
   193	
   194	That is a much clearer target than “humans” generally.
   195	
   196	### What each holdout establishes
   197	
   198	| Desired claim | What must be unavailable during development |
   199	|---|---|
   200	| New-task performance | Entire task identities; related variants should stay together |
   201	| New-agent performance | The held-out agent’s labeled outputs, including during validation |
   202	| New-human performance | All labels from the held-out people |
   203	| All three simultaneously | Test examples combining held-out tasks, an excluded agent, and held-out humans |
   204	
   205	Randomly splitting \(R_{tah}\) cells can leave the same task, agent, human, and even candidate artifact on both sides. That does not test the generalization you described.
   206	
   207	Also, repeated optimization against validation scores makes that validation set part of development. Keep a final test set untouched after selecting prompts, models, calibration, and reporting thresholds. Model selection can itself overfit finite validation data. [jmlr.org](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
   208	
   209	### Why there is no universally sufficient \(T,A,H\)
   210	
   211	The coworker’s three-letter equation becomes useful once interpreted as **uncertainty in an estimated average loss**, rather than the judge’s actual error.
   212	
   213	For illustration, suppose we have a balanced, fully crossed study and a random-effects model with independent task, agent, human, and interaction effects. Writing \(T,A,H\) for the **evaluation-set counts** in this equation,
   214	
   215	\[
   216	\begin{aligned}
   217	\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mathcal L})
   218	={}&
   219	\frac{\sigma_T^2}{T}
   220	+
   221	\frac{\sigma_A^2}{A}
   222	+
   223	\frac{\sigma_H^2}{H}\\
   224	&+
   225	\frac{\sigma_{TA}^2}{TA}
   226	+
   227	\frac{\sigma_{TH}^2}{TH}
   228	+
   229	\frac{\sigma_{AH}^2}{AH}
   230	+
   231	\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{res}}^2}{TAH}.
   232	\end{aligned}
   233	\]
   234	
   235	Here \(\mathcal L\) is mean judging loss, and the variance components describe how that loss changes across tasks, agents, people, and their combinations.
   236	
   237	This explains the allocation decision:
   238	
   239	- Large task variability calls for more distinct tasks.
   240	- Large human variability calls for more distinct humans.
   241	- Large agent variability calls for more different systems.
   242	- Large generation variability calls for additional outputs from the same task–agent pairs.
   243	
   244	**Thousands of reviews by the same five people do not become thousands of independent samples of people.**
   245	
   246	For a sparse assignment design, use the actual assignment structure rather than mechanically substituting counts into the balanced formula. Uncertainty calculations must respect the crossed dependence; naïvely bootstrapping individual ratings can be misleading. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.1111?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
   247	
   248	### How a pilot turns this into a human-count decision
   249	
   250	Suppose a pilot estimates that the standard deviation of human-specific average-loss effects is \(\sigma_H=0.10\). The human component of a normal-approximation 95% half-width would be
   251	
   252	\[
   253	w_H\approx1.96\frac{\sigma_H}{\sqrt{H_{\mathrm{test}}}}.
   254	\]
   255	
   256	That gives:
   257	
   258	| Distinct held-out humans | Approximate human component of the half-width |
   259	|---:|---:|
   260	| 6 | 0.080 |
   261	| 16 | 0.049 |
   262	
   263	Equivalently,
   264	
   265	\[
   266	H_{\mathrm{test}}
   267	\gtrsim
   268	\left(\frac{1.96\sigma_H}{w_H}\right)^2.
   269	\]
   270	
   271	**These are illustrative calculations, not measured variance estimates.** They concern only the human component, not the entire interval; small-sample intervals can also be wider.
   272	
   273	This is the justification I would use for choosing \(H\): estimate the relevant variance, specify acceptable precision, and calculate the required count. If the human-effect SD doubles, maintaining the same precision requires about four times as many humans under this model.
   274	
   275	### What a conservative three-dimension bound says
   276	
   277	There is also a useful theoretical check. In an idealized complete-grid experiment, assume:
   278	
   279	- A frozen judge;
   280	- Independent iid samples of task, agent, and human identities;
   281	- A bounded loss in \([0,1]\), determined by those identities.
   282	
   283	Changing one task, agent, or human changes the grid-average loss by at most \(1/T\), \(1/A\), or \(1/H\). McDiarmid’s inequality then gives
   284	
   285	\[
   286	\boxed{
   287	\mathcal L
   288	\le
   289	\widehat{\mathcal L}
   290	+
   291	\sqrt{
   292	\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}2
   293	\left(\frac1T+\frac1A+\frac1H\right)
   294	}
   295	}
   296	\]
   297	
   298	with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Additional random generation and rating steps require accounting for their randomness too. [people.eecs.berkeley.edu](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~bartlett/courses/281b-sp08/13.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
   299	
   300	This bound is deliberately conservative. Its value here is to show why a large product \(TAH\) does not automatically imply strong generalization across all three dimensions.
   301	
   302	It also exposes the limitation of \(A=4\): **four named systems provide limited evidence about a population of future systems**, regardless of how many task outputs you collect. Furthermore, the four systems you deliberately select are not automatically iid samples from such a population.
   303	
   304	### My revised concrete starting design
   305	
   306	For the broader goal you now describe, I recommend the following **initial budget**, adjusted after a pilot.
   307	
   308	I am still using **896 as the task count from your supplied plan**, conditional on that being the size of the chosen benchmark release.
   309	
   310	| Quantity | Starting recommendation |
   311	|---|---|
   312	| \(|T|\): benchmark tasks | **896, all included in the final audit** |
   313	| Development task split | **64 training + 64 validation** |
   314	| Tasks untouched during development | **768** |
   315	| \(|A|\): required agent configurations | **4: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Grok**, with configurations frozen |
   316	| \(|H|\): distinct qualified people | **24 total: 8 development + 16 untouched audit experts** |
   317	| \(m\): ratings per artifact | **3 randomly assigned distinct humans** |
   318	| Dense distribution-diagnostic subset | **128 randomly selected untouched tasks**, all four agents, **8 ratings per artifact** |
   319	| Final candidate outputs | **One fresh output per task–agent pair initially** |
   320	
   321	Why these choices?
   322	
   323	**64 training and 64 validation tasks** are a starting allocation for prompt/model/calibration selection with an already pretrained judge. They provide 512 development artifacts across four agents while preserving a large unseen-task test set. They are not a demonstrated sample-complexity requirement for training a new model. Expand development data if learning curves warrant it, before inspecting the final test results.
   324	
   325	**24 humans instead of five** reflects your changed target. More independent people help assess transfer across people. Sparse ratings keep their workloads manageable. The eight development raters can support grouped human cross-validation during selection; the sixteen audit raters remain entirely separate.
   326	
   327	**Three ratings per artifact** support estimation of the proper-loss objective. The denser subset provides better diagnostics of disagreement and conditional rating distributions. Neither three nor eight votes should be described as the exact distribution of the entire expert population.
   328	
   329	### Annotation budget
   330	
   331	| Component | Reviews |
   332	|---|---:|
   333	| Development | \(128\times4\times3=1{,}536\) |
   334	| Final audit across all tasks and agents | \(896\times4\times3=10{,}752\) |
   335	| Add five ratings on the dense subset, bringing each artifact from three to eight | \(128\times4\times5=2{,}560\) |
   336	| **Total** | **14,848 reviews** |
   337	
   338	This is fewer reviews than my earlier 28,160 proposal, while involving more distinct humans. With balanced assignment, each audit expert would perform about **832 reviews**. That remains a substantial commitment, so the pilot should measure review time as well as variability.
   339	
   340	The change is possible because a proper-loss evaluation uses individual votes directly; it does not require every expert to rate every artifact.
   341	
   342	### How to test agent transfer with the four required agents
   343	
   344	Evaluate two things separately:
   345	
   346	1. **The main judge**, developed using all four agents’ development outputs.
   347	2. **Four leave-one-agent-out judges**, each developed without one agent’s labeled outputs in either training or validation.
   348	
   349	Evaluate each excluded-agent judge on:
   350	
   351	\[
   352	\boxed{
   353	768\text{ untouched tasks}
   354	\times
   355	\text{the excluded agent}
   356	\times
   357	\text{untouched audit humans}.
   358	}
   359	\]
   360	
   361	Each fold therefore tests all three unseen dimensions simultaneously. The same collected audit labels can be reused, so these additional judge fits need not multiply annotation costs.
   362	
   363	The supported claim would be:
   364	
   365	> The judging procedure transferred to each of the four evaluated agent configurations when developed on the other three.
   366	
   367	This evaluates the **development procedure**. It does not independently validate a final judge trained on all four against arbitrary future agents. A prospective evaluation on a genuinely new system or release would strengthen that claim.
   368	
   369	### What happens to the earlier “approximately 0.05” margin?
   370	
   371	For independent bounded artifact-level losses **conditional on a fixed panel/protocol**, the 768-task calculation is
   372	
   373	\[
   374	\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/0.05)}{2(768)}}\approx0.0534.
   375	\]
   376	
   377	That explains why preserving a large unseen-task set is attractive. But **this is not the total uncertainty for the new population-level design**. Human selection, task-family dependence, and claims about unseen agents require their own treatment.
   378	
   379	I would not present the old 0.04945 margin as a guarantee of distribution matching across new tasks, agents, and humans.
   380	
   381	## 3. What would make a reviewer or committee believe this?
   382	
   383	I would organize the evidence around four explicit questions.
   384	
   385	### A. Does the objective measure the stated target?
   386	
   387	Present the RPS decomposition above. It establishes that the loss targets the complete conditional human-rating distribution.
   388	
   389	Keep individual ratings, including disagreements. Do not replace them all with an adjudicated consensus score and then claim to have modeled disagreement. Research on annotation disagreement supports preserving information that majority-vote labels can discard, although formal-specification grading needs its own validation. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.6/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
   390	
   391	Also distinguish:
   392	
   393	- **Predicted rating spread:** should reflect human disagreement.
   394	- **Instability across repeated judge calls:** should be small enough for dependable use.
   395	
   396	A stable probability vector can correctly predict substantial human disagreement.
   397	
   398	### B. Does the learned judge improve on independent data?
   399	
   400	At minimum, compare:
   401	
   402	| Method | Purpose |
   403	|---|---|
   404	| Constant rating-distribution baseline | Detects whether the judge uses submission-specific information |

   445	This is essential for VeriBench. Humans and the AI could agree because they share the same mistaken reference or grading shortcut.
   446	
   447	Add a separately reported set of controlled specification changes:
   448	
   449	| Change | Expected response |
   450	|---|---|
   451	| Remove a necessary specification obligation | Coverage should decrease |
   452	| Strengthen a precondition to exclude required difficult inputs | Coverage/domain score should decrease |
   453	| Replace a specification with a semantically equivalent formulation | Score should remain similar |
   454	| Add irrelevant or vacuous statements | They should not earn meaningful coverage credit |
   455	| Supply a faulty or incomplete reference | The judge should expose the discrepancy where possible |
   456	| Preserve the specifications while changing proof completion | Coverage should remain distinct from proof completion |
   457	
   458	Use mechanically checked implications or counterexamples where available to establish the expected relationship. A correct but unproven specification should not lose coverage credit merely because its proof is absent.
   459	
   460	This connects “matches experts” to the capability you actually want to measure.
   461	
   462	### How I would frame the contribution
   463	
   464	I would frame the study as:
   465	
   466	> We develop a reference-assisted probabilistic judge of formal-specification coverage, optimize it using a proper ordinal scoring loss, and evaluate transfer to held-out tasks, experts, and agent configurations. Controlled specification perturbations assess whether agreement with experts tracks the intended semantic properties.
   467	
   468	The proper scoring rule itself is established methodology. Your contribution would be the **effective formal-specification judge, the expert-rated evaluation data, and credible evidence of semantic validity and transfer**.
   469	
   470	A reviewer does not need a promise about every future agent or every possible expert. They need a clearly defined target, an appropriate objective, an honest independent evaluation, and results strong enough to support the stated scope.
   471	
   472	## TL;DR
   473	
   474	1. **Your intuition is right when the distributions are matched conditional on the same submission.** Pooled histograms or moments can match perfectly while every judgment is wrong.
   475	2. **Use probabilistic ordinal learning.** Forward KL/cross-entropy is justified; I recommend RPS because it respects the ordered 0–5 scale and is bounded. Its excess expected loss equals a distance between conditional rating distributions.
   476	3. **Your broader generalization goal changes the human design.** My starting recommendation is **all 896 tasks, four agent configurations, and 24 experts: eight development plus sixteen held out**.
   477	4. **Start with 64 training tasks, 64 validation tasks, and 768 untouched tasks.** Collect three ratings per artifact, with eight ratings on a random 128-task audit subset: **14,848 reviews**.
   478	5. **Those are planning numbers, not proven sufficient counts.** Use pilot variance and prespecified precision requirements to revise them. Run leave-one-agent-out experiments for joint transfer, and retain semantic checks so that human agreement supports the actual formal-specification claim.

=====01_abstract.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: Abstract distinguishes a prospective protocol from historical evidence.
     2	\begin{abstract}
     3	% Context and problem.
     4	Artificial intelligence (AI) judges are useful evaluation instruments only to the extent that their ratings measure the intended property.
     5	For formal specification coverage, a high correlation with experts does not establish agreement about score levels or disagreement between experts on individual artifacts.
     6	% Proposed approach.
     7	We specify a study in which a judge predicts the six-category human-rating distribution conditional on Python source, a candidate Lean formalization, and a gold reference.
     8	The primary objective is normalized ranked probability score, with correlations and absolute error retained as diagnostics.
     9	% Concrete design and evidence status.
    10	A prospective design covers 896 benchmark tasks and four solver configurations, with 24 distinct experts and a starting budget of 14,848 individual ratings.
    11	Separate task, solver, and expert holdouts test different transfer claims, while controlled specification changes test whether human agreement reflects the intended construct.
    12	Historical VeriBench evidence motivates the design: a 30-artifact, ten-task test has Spearman correlation 0.826, but its 95\% task-bootstrap interval is [0.316, 0.966] and its normalized mean bias is +0.181.
    13	% Scope and limitation.
    14	Those previously exposed data do not validate the proposed judge; fresh human collection and the prospective results remain pending.
    15	The contribution is a reproducible measurement protocol that separates predictive agreement, semantic validity, and uncertainty about both.
    16	\end{abstract}
=====02_introduction.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: Motivate evaluating the measurement instrument and state the prospective contribution.
     2	\section{Introduction}
     3	% Move 1: concrete research context.
     4	AI agents increasingly produce artifacts whose quality cannot be reduced to whether their code executes.
     5	A formalization agent, for example, can produce a Lean program and prove every theorem it states while omitting a required property of the original Python program.
     6	An evaluation instrument must distinguish successful proof construction from adequate specification of the task.
     7	This distinction matters when scientific agents use formal artifacts as evidence: correctness of a weak claim does not establish completeness of the intended claim.
     8	
     9	% Move 2: existing practice and its useful contribution.
    10	Large language models (LLMs) can compare candidate artifacts with instructions and references at a scale that expert review cannot easily match.
    11	Prior work on LLM judges demonstrates useful human agreement while identifying position, verbosity, and self-preference effects \citep{zheng2023judging}.
    12	In the present setting, the immediate target is formal specification coverage (FSC): whether candidate theorem statements express the properties required by the task, potentially through logical implication rather than textual similarity.
    13	Human ratings provide an operational comparison for this semantic assessment.
    14	
    15	% Move 3: the remaining measurement problem.
    16	Correlation alone leaves the central question unresolved.
    17	A judge can preserve the ordering of artifacts while systematically assigning higher scores than experts.
    18	Two judges can also have identical pooled score distributions while assigning those scores to different artifacts.
    19	Furthermore, averaging all expert ratings into one target erases whether a particular artifact produces consensus or disagreement.
    20	These are distinct failures, and collecting more ratings does not repair the choice of an unsuitable objective.
    21	
    22	% Move 4: central approach.
    23	We therefore define the target as a conditional distribution over six ordinal human ratings and evaluate probability forecasts with a proper scoring rule.
    24	The judge receives the source program, candidate formalization, and reference, together with a fixed rubric.
    25	It predicts how qualified experts following that rubric would distribute their ratings.
    26	Normalized ranked probability score (RPS) gives an explicit objective for this target; correlations remain useful summaries of expected scores, rather than a substitute for distributional agreement.
    27	
    28	% Move 5: concrete contribution.
    29	This paper specifies the corresponding data collection, selection, and evaluation protocol.
    30	It distinguishes the number of tasks, the number of solver configurations, the total number of human participants, and the number of ratings assigned to an artifact.
    31	The starting design covers all 896 tasks of a fixed VeriBench release and four named solver configurations, while preserving separate evidence for unseen tasks, excluded solver configurations, and unseen experts.
    32	We also preserve historical judge results with their uncertainty and exposure limitations instead of treating them as fresh validation.
    33	
    34	% Move 6: scope and evidence status.
    35	The contribution is a prospective methodology and historical case study, not a completed claim that a new judge works.
    36	Proper scoring rules and dependence-aware inference are established tools; our contribution is their operational use for FSC, with auditable inputs, splits, controls, and a collection budget.
    37	The project concerns AI, agent, and LLM judges.
    38	A separate prover judge may use AI to search for an implication proof, but the proof checker determines whether that implication was established.
    39	Human agreement and a checked proof answer different questions, and a proof-search timeout establishes neither equivalence nor non-entailment.
=====03_target.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: Define inputs, the human population, and ordinal forecasts without conflating proof validity.
     2	\section{Target and Measurement Conditions}
     3	\label{sec:target}
     4	For task $t$ and solver configuration $a$, let
     5	\begin{equation}
     6	 z_{ta}=(x_t,\widehat y_{ta},y_t^*),
     7	 \qquad R_{tah}\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.
     8	\end{equation}
     9	Here $x_t$ is the original Python source and task contract, $\widehat y_{ta}$ is the candidate Lean artifact, $y_t^*$ is the reference, and $h$ identifies a human rater.
    10	The normalized scalar rating is $R_{tah}/5$.
    11	The three inputs must have identical content for humans and the judge; the rendered view and proof visibility are recorded separately.
    12	
    13	\subsection{What coverage means}
    14	A formal specification is a theorem statement considered without its proof.
    15	Coverage concerns the required statements and the domains and assumptions under which they hold.
    16	A candidate may cover a reference statement with a stronger statement or with several statements together.
    17	Counting theorem names or measuring textual overlap cannot establish this implication.
    18	Conversely, narrowing a precondition can remove required cases even when a theorem's conclusion is unchanged.
    19	Proof completion is recorded separately from statement coverage.
    20	
    21	The source program constrains the intended behavior but does not automatically resolve a conflict between implementation behavior, task requirements, and the reference.
    22	The protocol records such conflicts for independent inspection rather than silently choosing one input as infallible.
    23	Conditioning on a reference makes the rating task more concrete; it can also make both humans and a judge prefer the reference's representation.
    24	Reference sensitivity is therefore a measurement condition to test, not an assumed benefit of adding the reference.
    25	
    26	\subsection{The human distribution}
    27	Let $\mathcal H$ denote a specified population of qualified Lean and formal-methods experts using the same rubric.
    28	The target is the probability mass function
    29	\begin{equation}
    30	 p^*(r\mid z)=\Pr_{h\sim\mathcal H}(R_h(z)=r).
    31	\end{equation}
    32	This definition requires a recruitment frame and a rating procedure, including allowed assistance, time guidance, and treatment of ambiguous inputs.
    33	It does not make a convenience sample representative of all experts.
    34	The empirical distribution from a fixed recruited panel is a different, narrower target; both must be labeled when reported.
    35	
    36	The judge predicts $q_\theta(r\mid z)$, a nonnegative vector of six probabilities summing to one.
    37	Its expected normalized rating is $\mu_q(z)=\sum_{r=0}^5(r/5)q_\theta(r\mid z)$.
    38	Each individual human rating is retained, including disagreement.
    39	A histogram of stochastic scalar judge outputs does not by itself represent the human distribution: model-call instability and human disagreement have different sources.
    40	The proposed probability-vector interface is consequently a new judge condition, not a reinterpretation of an old scalar score.
=====04_objective.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: State and derive the proper ordinal objective and its relation to distribution error.
     2	\section{A Distribution-Sensitive Objective}
     3	\label{sec:objective}
     4	Proper scoring rules reward accurate probability forecasts in expectation \citep{gneiting2007strictly}.
     5	For the cumulative probabilities $Q_c=\sum_{r=0}^c q_r$, we use the loss
     6	\begin{equation}
     7	 S(q,r)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}
     8	       \bigl(Q_c-\mathbf{1}\{r\leq c\}\bigr)^2.
     9	 \label{eq:rps}
    10	\end{equation}
    11	The factor $1/5$ places RPS on $[0,1]$.
    12	The ordered thresholds retain the ordinal structure: probability placed many categories away from an observed rating incurs more cumulative error than probability placed in an adjacent category.
    13	Equal threshold weights are an explicit design choice, not a claim that every practical consequence of a rating is equally spaced.
    14	
    15	Let $P_c=\Pr(R\leq c\mid z)$.
    16	For each threshold, expansion of the squared error gives
    17	\begin{align}
    18	 \mathbb E[S(q,R)\mid z]
    19	 &=D(q,p^*)+U(p^*),\\
    20	 D(q,p^*)&=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}(Q_c-P_c)^2,\\
    21	 U(p^*)&=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}P_c(1-P_c).
    22	 \label{eq:decomposition}
    23	\end{align}
    24	The first term measures conditional distribution error; the second is the loss remaining even for a perfect forecast of a disagreeing expert population.
    25	Because the cumulative probabilities determine all six category probabilities, the unrestricted expected-loss minimizer is uniquely $q=p^*$.
    26	This fact justifies the target of selection.
    27	It does not guarantee that a particular model class, prompt search, or finite sample will attain that target.
    28	
    29	For equal category spacing on $[0,1]$, the one-dimensional Wasserstein distance is
    30	\begin{equation}
    31	 W_1(q,p^*)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}|Q_c-P_c|.
    32	\end{equation}
    33	Cauchy--Schwarz gives $W_1(q,p^*)^2\leq D(q,p^*)$.
    34	Thus small excess expected RPS bounds an interpretable distribution distance.
    35	More generally, for a normalized $L$-Lipschitz utility function $f$, the expectation gap is at most $L W_1$.
    36	This connects a distributional claim to uses such as estimating the mean rating, without requiring a separate match of every moment.
    37	
    38	\subsection{Why correlation or a pooled divergence is insufficient}
    39	Consider human scores $(0,0.25,0.5)$ and judge scores $(0.5,0.75,1)$.
    40	Pearson and rank correlations are one, although every score differs by $0.5$.
    41	Alternatively, permuting predictions among artifacts preserves the marginal score histogram while destroying itemwise agreement.
    42	A divergence between pooled histograms misses that failure.
    43	The required comparison is conditional on the same artifact, then averaged across artifacts.
    44	
    45	Logarithmic loss is another proper objective and connects to Kullback--Leibler divergence, but it ignores category order and diverges when the judge assigns zero probability to an observed category.
    46	With few ratings per artifact, directly estimating an entire human probability vector and plugging it into a divergence is also noisy.
    47	RPS can instead score each individual rating without declaring a sparse empirical histogram to be the true human distribution.
    48	We retain logarithmic loss only as an optional prespecified sensitivity analysis with a documented probability-floor policy.
    49	
    50	\subsection{Selection and artifact weighting}
    51	For $n$ artifacts, with assigned rater set $\mathcal H_i$ of size $m_i$, define
    52	\begin{equation}
    53	 \widehat L(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}
    54	       \frac1{m_i}\sum_{h\in\mathcal H_i}S(q_\theta(z_i),R_{ih}).
    55	 \label{eq:empirical}
    56	\end{equation}
    57	Candidate construction uses training data; selection minimizes this loss on validation data.
    58	Artifacts receiving additional diagnostic ratings retain the same total weight as other artifacts.
    59	All candidates, prompt changes, and fitted score mappings are recorded because repeated model selection can overfit a validation criterion \citep{cawley2010overfitting}.
    60	Final test ratings do not enter this process.
=====05_design.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: Prospective counts separate artifact instances, identities, and transfer claims.
     2	\section{Prospective Study Design}
     3	\label{sec:design}
     4	The starting population is the fixed public VeriBench release \texttt{veribench@1.3}, containing 896 Python tasks.
     5	The data source is pinned to commit \texttt{c9dfd8e} of the public Harbor dataset collection \citep{veribenchrelease}.
     6	Task contents, reference versions, instruction version, and toolchain must be hashed before collection.
     7	The four required solver configurations are Claude Code, Codex, a Gemini agent, and a Grok agent.
     8	These names define the intended panel; exact model versions, harnesses, tools, effort, and budgets remain to be frozen.
     9	They are deliberately selected configurations, not random draws from every possible future solver.
    10	
    11	\subsection{Task and human allocation}
    12	The initial allocation is 64 training tasks, 64 validation tasks, and 768 held-out tasks.
    13	Related task variants and near-duplicates are grouped before splitting.
    14	If those groups prevent the exact counts, the allocation and budget must be amended before test inspection.
    15	We recruit 24 qualified experts: eight for training and validation, and 16 different people for the final audit.
    16	Each artifact receives three independently submitted ratings from distinct randomly assigned people in the relevant pool.
    17	Assignment balances workload and maintains overlap between people; it is recorded rather than inferred from a dense tensor.
    18	
    19	The final audit covers all 896 task identities with fresh solver generations.
    20	Consequently, its 128 previously seen tasks answer a fresh-output question, while its 768 held-out tasks answer a task-transfer question.
    21	Those strata are reported separately even when a full-benchmark mean is also useful.
    22	One solver output per task--configuration cell is collected initially in each stage, without selecting the best of retries.
    23	This design does not estimate generation variance at a fixed cell.
    24	Repeated identical bytes remain distinct generation records but do not create evidence of independent content.
    25	
    26	We randomly select 128 of the held-out tasks before observing their ratings and collect eight total ratings for each of their four artifacts.
    27	These additional five ratings support distribution diagnostics; they do not make the empirical category histogram exact.
    28	Table~\ref{tab:budget} distinguishes new artifacts from additional ratings of an existing artifact.
    29	The resulting workload is 192 reviews per training/validation participant and 832 per audit participant under exact balancing.
    30	These are planned counts, not measured or assumed feasible time commitments.
    31	
    32	\begin{table}[t]
    33	\centering
    34	\begin{tabular}{lrr}
    35	\toprule
    36	Collection stage & Artifacts & Ratings \\
    37	\midrule
    38	128 tasks $\times$ 4, train/validation & 512 & 1,536 \\
    39	896 tasks $\times$ 4, final audit & 3,584 & 10,752 \\
    40	Extra five on 128 $\times$ 4 audit files & 0 & 2,560 \\
    41	\midrule
    42	Total & 4,096 & 14,848 \\
    43	\bottomrule
    44	\end{tabular}
    45	\caption{Prospective collection budget, not collected data.
    46	The two stages have separate generations and disjoint human pools.
    47	Three ratings are assigned initially to every artifact; the dense subset has eight in total.}
    48	\label{tab:budget}
    49	\end{table}
    50	
    51	\subsection{What is held out}
    52	The main judge is trained and selected with all four configurations' training and validation outputs.
    53	Its audit establishes performance on the evaluated configurations, with separate new-task and new-human evidence.
    54	It cannot also establish that these same configurations were unseen by that judge.
    55	
    56	To test transfer to each excluded configuration, we fit four additional judges.
    57	For each fit, one configuration's outputs, ratings, and prompt examples are excluded from both training and validation.
    58	The fit is evaluated on that configuration's 768 held-out tasks using audit raters.
    59	All four fits reuse the same collected audit ratings.
    60	These experiments test the transfer of the training/selection procedure, not a single judge that somehow treats all four training configurations as unseen.
    61	They also do not establish transfer to arbitrary future model versions.
    62	Historical task and solver exposure is recorded; a new split cannot erase earlier prompt design or unknown pretraining exposure.
    63	
    64	The final human pool supplies no ratings for judge selection.
    65	An analysis conditional on the 16 recruited audit experts can establish agreement with that panel.
    66	An inference about a wider expert population additionally requires a defensible recruitment and sampling model.
    67	Holding out identities reduces direct leakage but does not by itself make either experts or solver configurations representative.
    68	
    69	\subsection{Pilot and frozen execution}
    70	A training/validation-only pilot measures rating time, disagreement, fatigue, failure rates, and variance of paired losses.
    71	It also traces one artifact through generation, extraction, human display, judge input, probability parsing, and scoring using content hashes.
    72	Before final ratings are opened, we freeze the rubric, assignments, judge versions, analysis, repeat count, failure policy, endpoints, and practical tolerances.
    73	Task and participant exclusions, parser errors, missing outputs, and timeouts remain in the accounting.
    74	The plan is not a completed preregistration: practical thresholds and the feasibility of the proposed workload remain unresolved.

    11	The three inputs must have identical content for humans and the judge; the rendered view and proof visibility are recorded separately.
    12	
    13	\subsection{What coverage means}
    14	A formal specification is a theorem statement considered without its proof.
    15	Coverage concerns the required statements and the domains and assumptions under which they hold.
    16	A candidate may cover a reference statement with a stronger statement or with several statements together.
    17	Counting theorem names or measuring textual overlap cannot establish this implication.
    18	Conversely, narrowing a precondition can remove required cases even when a theorem's conclusion is unchanged.
    19	Proof completion is recorded separately from statement coverage.
    20	
    21	The source program constrains the intended behavior but does not automatically resolve a conflict between implementation behavior, task requirements, and the reference.
    22	The protocol records such conflicts for independent inspection rather than silently choosing one input as infallible.
    23	Conditioning on a reference makes the rating task more concrete; it can also make both humans and a judge prefer the reference's representation.
    24	Reference sensitivity is therefore a measurement condition to test, not an assumed benefit of adding the reference.
    25	
    26	\subsection{The human distribution}
    27	Let $\mathcal H$ denote a specified population of qualified Lean and formal-methods experts using the same rubric.
    28	The target is the probability mass function
    29	\begin{equation}
    30	 p^*(r\mid z)=\Pr_{h\sim\mathcal H}(R_h(z)=r).
    31	\end{equation}
    32	This definition requires a recruitment frame and a rating procedure, including allowed assistance, time guidance, and treatment of ambiguous inputs.
    33	It does not make a convenience sample representative of all experts.
    34	The empirical distribution from a fixed recruited panel is a different, narrower target; both must be labeled when reported.
    35	
    36	The judge predicts $q_\theta(r\mid z)$, a nonnegative vector of six probabilities summing to one.
    37	Its expected normalized rating is $\mu_q(z)=\sum_{r=0}^5(r/5)q_\theta(r\mid z)$.
    38	Each individual human rating is retained, including disagreement.
    39	A histogram of stochastic scalar judge outputs does not by itself represent the human distribution: model-call instability and human disagreement have different sources.
    40	The proposed probability-vector interface is consequently a new judge condition, not a reinterpretation of an old scalar score.
=====04_objective.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: State and derive the proper ordinal objective and its relation to distribution error.
     2	\section{A Distribution-Sensitive Objective}
     3	\label{sec:objective}
     4	Proper scoring rules reward accurate probability forecasts in expectation \citep{gneiting2007strictly}.
     5	For the cumulative probabilities $Q_c=\sum_{r=0}^c q_r$, we use the loss
     6	\begin{equation}
     7	 S(q,r)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}
     8	       \bigl(Q_c-\mathbf{1}\{r\leq c\}\bigr)^2.
     9	 \label{eq:rps}
    10	\end{equation}
    11	The factor $1/5$ places RPS on $[0,1]$.
    12	The ordered thresholds retain the ordinal structure: probability placed many categories away from an observed rating incurs more cumulative error than probability placed in an adjacent category.
    13	Equal threshold weights are an explicit design choice, not a claim that every practical consequence of a rating is equally spaced.
    14	
    15	Let $P_c=\Pr(R\leq c\mid z)$.
    16	For each threshold, expansion of the squared error gives
    17	\begin{align}
    18	 \mathbb E[S(q,R)\mid z]
    19	 &=D(q,p^*)+U(p^*),\\
    20	 D(q,p^*)&=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}(Q_c-P_c)^2,\\
    21	 U(p^*)&=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}P_c(1-P_c).
    22	 \label{eq:decomposition}
    23	\end{align}
    24	The first term measures conditional distribution error; the second is the loss remaining even for a perfect forecast of a disagreeing expert population.
    25	Because the cumulative probabilities determine all six category probabilities, the unrestricted expected-loss minimizer is uniquely $q=p^*$.
    26	This fact justifies the target of selection.
    27	It does not guarantee that a particular model class, prompt search, or finite sample will attain that target.
    28	
    29	For equal category spacing on $[0,1]$, the one-dimensional Wasserstein distance is
    30	\begin{equation}
    31	 W_1(q,p^*)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{c=0}^{4}|Q_c-P_c|.
    32	\end{equation}
    33	Cauchy--Schwarz gives $W_1(q,p^*)^2\leq D(q,p^*)$.
    34	Thus small excess expected RPS bounds an interpretable distribution distance.
    35	More generally, for a normalized $L$-Lipschitz utility function $f$, the expectation gap is at most $L W_1$.
    36	This connects a distributional claim to uses such as estimating the mean rating, without requiring a separate match of every moment.
    37	
    38	\subsection{Why correlation or a pooled divergence is insufficient}
    39	Consider human scores $(0,0.25,0.5)$ and judge scores $(0.5,0.75,1)$.
    40	Pearson and rank correlations are one, although every score differs by $0.5$.
    41	Alternatively, permuting predictions among artifacts preserves the marginal score histogram while destroying itemwise agreement.
    42	A divergence between pooled histograms misses that failure.
    43	The required comparison is conditional on the same artifact, then averaged across artifacts.
    44	
    45	Logarithmic loss is another proper objective and connects to Kullback--Leibler divergence, but it ignores category order and diverges when the judge assigns zero probability to an observed category.
    46	With few ratings per artifact, directly estimating an entire human probability vector and plugging it into a divergence is also noisy.
    47	RPS can instead score each individual rating without declaring a sparse empirical histogram to be the true human distribution.
    48	We retain logarithmic loss only as an optional prespecified sensitivity analysis with a documented probability-floor policy.
    49	
    50	\subsection{Selection and artifact weighting}
    51	For $n$ artifacts, with assigned rater set $\mathcal H_i$ of size $m_i$, define
    52	\begin{equation}
    53	 \widehat L(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}
    54	       \frac1{m_i}\sum_{h\in\mathcal H_i}S(q_\theta(z_i),R_{ih}).
    55	 \label{eq:empirical}
    56	\end{equation}
    57	Candidate construction uses training data; selection minimizes this loss on validation data.
    58	Artifacts receiving additional diagnostic ratings retain the same total weight as other artifacts.
    59	All candidates, prompt changes, and fitted score mappings are recorded because repeated model selection can overfit a validation criterion \citep{cawley2010overfitting}.
    60	Final test ratings do not enter this process.
=====05_design.tex=====
     1	% TLDR: Prospective counts separate artifact instances, identities, and transfer claims.
     2	\section{Prospective Study Design}
     3	\label{sec:design}
     4	The starting population is the fixed public VeriBench release \texttt{veribench@1.3}, containing 896 Python tasks.
     5	The data source is pinned to commit \texttt{c9dfd8e} of the public Harbor dataset collection \citep{veribenchrelease}.
     6	Task contents, reference versions, instruction version, and toolchain must be hashed before collection.
     7	The four required solver configurations are Claude Code, Codex, a Gemini agent, and a Grok agent.
     8	These names define the intended panel; exact model versions, harnesses, tools, effort, and budgets remain to be frozen.
     9	They are deliberately selected configurations, not random draws from every possible future solver.
    10	
    11	\subsection{Task and human allocation}
    12	The initial allocation is 64 training tasks, 64 validation tasks, and 768 held-out tasks.
    13	Related task variants and near-duplicates are grouped before splitting.
    14	If those groups prevent the exact counts, the allocation and budget must be amended before test inspection.
    15	We recruit 24 qualified experts: eight for training and validation, and 16 different people for the final audit.
    16	Each artifact receives three independently submitted ratings from distinct randomly assigned people in the relevant pool.
    17	Assignment balances workload and maintains overlap between people; it is recorded rather than inferred from a dense tensor.
    18	
    19	The final audit covers all 896 task identities with fresh solver generations.
    20	Consequently, its 128 previously seen tasks answer a fresh-output question, while its 768 held-out tasks answer a task-transfer question.
    21	Those strata are reported separately even when a full-benchmark mean is also useful.
    22	One solver output per task--configuration cell is collected initially in each stage, without selecting the best of retries.
    23	This design does not estimate generation variance at a fixed cell.
    24	Repeated identical bytes remain distinct generation records but do not create evidence of independent content.
    25	
    26	We randomly select 128 of the held-out tasks before observing their ratings and collect eight total ratings for each of their four artifacts.
    27	These additional five ratings support distribution diagnostics; they do not make the empirical category histogram exact.
    28	Table~\ref{tab:budget} distinguishes new artifacts from additional ratings of an existing artifact.
    29	The resulting workload is 192 reviews per training/validation participant and 832 per audit participant under exact balancing.
    30	These are planned counts, not measured or assumed feasible time commitments.
    31	
    32	\begin{table}[t]
    33	\centering
    34	\begin{tabular}{lrr}
    35	\toprule
    36	Collection stage & Artifacts & Ratings \\
    37	\midrule
    38	128 tasks $\times$ 4, train/validation & 512 & 1,536 \\
    39	896 tasks $\times$ 4, final audit & 3,584 & 10,752 \\
    40	Extra five on 128 $\times$ 4 audit files & 0 & 2,560 \\
    41	\midrule
    42	Total & 4,096 & 14,848 \\
    43	\bottomrule
    44	\end{tabular}
    45	\caption{Prospective collection budget, not collected data.
    46	The two stages have separate generations and disjoint human pools.
    47	Three ratings are assigned initially to every artifact; the dense subset has eight in total.}
    48	\label{tab:budget}
    49	\end{table}
    50	
    51	\subsection{What is held out}
    52	The main judge is trained and selected with all four configurations' training and validation outputs.
    53	Its audit establishes performance on the evaluated configurations, with separate new-task and new-human evidence.
    54	It cannot also establish that these same configurations were unseen by that judge.
    55	
    56	To test transfer to each excluded configuration, we fit four additional judges.
    57	For each fit, one configuration's outputs, ratings, and prompt examples are excluded from both training and validation.
    58	The fit is evaluated on that configuration's 768 held-out tasks using audit raters.
    59	All four fits reuse the same collected audit ratings.
    60	These experiments test the transfer of the training/selection procedure, not a single judge that somehow treats all four training configurations as unseen.
    61	They also do not establish transfer to arbitrary future model versions.
    62	Historical task and solver exposure is recorded; a new split cannot erase earlier prompt design or unknown pretraining exposure.
    63	
    64	The final human pool supplies no ratings for judge selection.
    65	An analysis conditional on the 16 recruited audit experts can establish agreement with that panel.
    66	An inference about a wider expert population additionally requires a defensible recruitment and sampling model.
    67	Holding out identities reduces direct leakage but does not by itself make either experts or solver configurations representative.
    68	
    69	\subsection{Pilot and frozen execution}
    70	A training/validation-only pilot measures rating time, disagreement, fatigue, failure rates, and variance of paired losses.
    71	It also traces one artifact through generation, extraction, human display, judge input, probability parsing, and scoring using content hashes.
    72	Before final ratings are opened, we freeze the rubric, assignments, judge versions, analysis, repeat count, failure policy, endpoints, and practical tolerances.
    73	Task and participant exclusions, parser errors, missing outputs, and timeouts remain in the accounting.
    74	The plan is not a completed preregistration: practical thresholds and the feasibility of the proposed workload remain unresolved.
