1	<!-- TLDR: This folder preserves historical VeriBench judge–human agreement aggregates and their limitations; it contains no new-study results or individual ratings. -->
2	# Historical VeriBench judge–human agreement
3	
4	**Doc link:** <https://github.com/brando90/trustworthy-theorem-judges/blob/main/experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/README.md>
5	
6	**TLDR:** Preserved historical scalar-judge evidence motivates a fresh study; it does not validate the new probability-output judge or a prover judge.
7	
8	**Status:** Historical evidence imported on 11-06-2026 from the committed VeriBench sources listed in [SOURCE_MANIFEST.json](SOURCE_MANIFEST.json).
9	The original files remain in their source project because its paper still cites them.
10	The new study has not collected or evaluated its fresh human data.
11	This archive concerns artificial intelligence (AI) / large language model (LLM) judges of formal specification coverage (FSC); it does not validate a prover-based judge.
12	
13	The remembered correlations around “0.6, 0.8, 0.8” most closely match experiment 100's **Kendall tau-b 0.698, Spearman rho 0.826, Pearson r 0.858**.
14	That is a later continued-paper result, distinct from the original paper's **Pearson r 0.703** and the subsequent automated recipe's **Spearman rho 0.603**.
15	
16	## Results kept separate
17	
18	| Historical condition | Scope and target | Spearman rho | Kendall tau-b | Pearson r |
19	|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
20	| Original two-fold task-split score-mapping analysis | 72 scored items from a 75-item, 25-task pool; one expert's two earlier-prompt passes averaged; validation folds, no test counterpart | 0.321143 | 0.265060 | 0.703349 |
21	| `100_karpathy_recipe_tc_judge_search_human_train_val_test`, selected judge | 30 candidate files, 10 test tasks; mean of available expert ratings | 0.825723 [0.316250, 0.965616] | 0.698217 [0.215512, 0.913038] | 0.857844 [0.706843, 0.941211] |
22	| Same selected judge, ordinary-reference subset | 24 candidate files, 8 test tasks; excludes two tasks whose references were placeholders at rating time | 0.651917 [−0.166241, 0.916077] | 0.513270 [−0.201404, 0.834547] | 0.834653 [0.453743, 0.957865] |
23	| `104_fsc_judge_5fold_cross_validation_all_75_expert_labels`, automated recipe, primary repetition, ties preserved | All 75 files, 25 tasks, five task-disjoint folds; each scored without its task in the training fold | 0.603 [0.287, 0.836] | 0.498 | 0.621 |
24	
25	Intervals are 95% percentile intervals resampling tasks, retaining their candidate files together.
26	Experiment 100 uses seed 20260928 and 10,000 requested draws for the full test; the ordinary subset uses 2,000 requested draws, with 1,998 nondegenerate draws for correlations and 2,000 for absolute agreement.
27	Experiment 104's tie-preserving addendum uses 10,000 task draws and seed 20260929.
28	P-values are not supplied by these imported receipts (`p-val=n/a`); no new significance test was performed.
29	The original aggregate CSV contains no confidence intervals; its continued-paper prose reports a Pearson interval [0.564, 0.804], but this import does not assert that it uses the later task-bootstrap method.
30	
31	## The selected judge and the human target
32	
33	The experiment 100 judge sees the Python source, candidate Lean file and reference Lean file at the versions shown to the human raters.
34	It uses their rating instructions, four conventions derived from training-split errors, and four expert-rated examples from other training tasks.
35	Its historical model routes are `openai/gpt-6-sol-high` with high reasoning effort and `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5-no-fallback` with maximum compute effort and adaptive thinking, through the Vals model gateway.
36	The score is the mean of two member medians, with three calls per member: six raw calls per completed judge score.
37	These are historical route identifiers, not a recommendation or authorization to run them today.
38	
39	The 25 tasks were split into 10 training, 5 validation and 10 test tasks, with all three candidate files of each task kept together.
40	The primary target is the mean of available ratings from a panel of three experts, divided by five.
41	Five people supplied ratings overall; the three-expert target must not be described as uniformly three ratings per item:
42	
43	| Split | Items with three expert ratings | Items with two expert ratings | Total items |
44	|---|---:|---:|---:|
45	| Training | 18 | 12 | 30 |
46	| Validation | 9 | 6 | 15 |
47	| Test | 18 | 12 | 30 |
48	| All | 45 | 30 | 75 |
49	
50	These counts were computed from the source's committed input manifest without importing individual ratings.
51	The candidate-generation provenance traces 74 of the 75 files to `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219`, temperature 0.7, three single-call zero-shot samples per Python task, without a tool or compiler loop.
52	One candidate lacks a generation receipt.
53	Thus the three candidates are generation samples, not three different solver systems, and these data do not establish transfer to frontier coding agents.
54	The generation prompt allowed missing proofs; these historical files must not be relabeled as outputs of the current prove-first solver contract.
55	
56	## Absolute agreement and variability
57	
58	All scores here are on [0, 1].
59	For experiment 100's full test:
60	
61	- Single-score absolute-agreement intraclass correlation, ICC(A,1): **0.727290 [0.391056, 0.890003]**.
62	- Consistency intraclass correlation, ICC(C,1): **0.851506**, with no interval in the imported receipt.
63	- Mean absolute error: **0.201111**.
64	- Mean bias, judge minus expert mean: **+0.181111**, from means **0.653333** and **0.472222**.
65	- Mean repeat standard deviation: **0.020488**; 90th percentile **0.057735**, maximum **0.173205**.
66	
67	The repeat statistic is computed from three **per-pass averages of the two models**, one call per member in each pass.
68	It is not the variability of independent repetitions of the complete six-call, median-based judge.
69	This distinction is explicit in the archived ensemble code.
70	The imported receipt has no uncertainty intervals for mean absolute error, mean bias, or repeat standard deviation.
71	
72	On the ordinary-reference subset, ICC(A,1) is **0.579786 [0.169238, 0.774305]**, mean absolute error **0.230556**, and mean bias **+0.205556** (judge **0.566667**, experts **0.361111**).
73	This exposes material uncertainty and score-level disagreement even though the all-item correlations are high.
74	
75	## Why the new study needs fresh data
76	
77	1. **Small independent task count.** The headline test has only ten task clusters; the ordinary-reference interval includes negative correlation.
78	2. **Reference versions and placeholder tasks.** Nine of the 25 reference files changed their theorem statements between rating and earlier judging. Five were placeholder references when rated. Experiment 100 restored rating-era inputs, but high scores on placeholder tasks contribute to its all-item correlation.
79	3. **Previously seen ratings.** The receipt discloses earlier exposure by experiments 75 and 83 and a descriptive initial audit. “One-shot test” refers to the selected candidate's test invocation, not a pristine dataset. The exact total number of judge versions that previously saw these ratings and the resulting selection inflation are not established by the imported receipt, explainer, or continued-paper appendix; no numerical inflation estimate is asserted.
80	4. **Single solver distribution.** Repeated samples from one older solver do not test transfer across agent families, tools, current model versions, or larger projects.
81	5. **Absolute score bias.** Correlation does not remove the positive mean bias or establish itemwise agreement.
82	6. **Human and judge repeat limits.** Two or three expert ratings per file and three paired-model passes provide limited evidence about conditional rating distributions and full-judge repeatability.
83	
84	These limitations motivate fresh task/agent/rater splits and distribution-sensitive metrics in the new methodology.
85	They are not problems that disappear merely by adding more correlated ratings to the same historical items.
86	
87	## Original paper versus later recipe
88	
89	The original **Pearson 0.703349** row uses a separate `gpt-5.3-codex` human-rubric judge with an isotonic score mapping fit on each training fold and evaluated on the disjoint validation fold.
90	Its raw zero-shot Pearson value is **0.515424** on the same archived 72-item target.
91	Judge and mapping choices used that validation protocol; there is no independent test-set counterpart.
92	The source paper reports that the raw scorer package is unavailable, so this archive preserves the aggregate record rather than claiming a complete executable reproduction.
93	
94	Experiment 104 evaluates an **automated recipe**, with fold-specific model-written conventions and examples and five calls per member, rather than the frozen experiment 100 judge.
95	Its original raw-float aggregate gives Spearman **0.601533 [0.285578, 0.834392]**, usually written **0.602**.
96	The published addendum rounds predictions before ranking to preserve mathematical ties and reports **0.603 [0.287, 0.836]**; use that figure when citing the continued paper.
97	The original excerpt is retained as provenance and must not silently overwrite the corrected figure.
98	The same addendum changes the second-repetition Spearman from **0.654** to **0.660**.
99	Its original two-repetition mean is not relabeled as a tie-corrected result.
100	
101	## Artifact inventory and reproducibility
102	
103	- [exp100_TEST_RECEIPT.json](exp100_TEST_RECEIPT.json): byte-exact original aggregate receipt; no per-item ratings.
104	- [original_cv2_aggregate_results.csv](original_cv2_aggregate_results.csv): byte-exact original aggregate results, including the 0.703349 row.
105	- [exp104_original_aggregate_excerpt.json](exp104_original_aggregate_excerpt.json): selected aggregate fields only; per-item arrays and other fields deliberately omitted.
106	- [exp104_tie_preserving_addendum.md](exp104_tie_preserving_addendum.md): byte-exact suffix extracted from the source report, explicitly labeled as an extraction in the manifest.
107	- [SOURCE_MANIFEST.json](SOURCE_MANIFEST.json): immutable source commit, source-file SHA-256 hashes, extraction descriptions and aggregate missingness counts.
108	
109	Frozen receipts retain their original spelling and format rather than receiving new comments or terminology edits.
110	No candidate Lean files, reference files, individual ratings, rater identities, contact information, or new sealed ratings are included.
111	The source repository is private; paths and hashes document provenance without publishing its contents beyond these authorized aggregates.
112	
113	## Post hoc error intervals, 11-06-2026
114	
115	The historical receipt has no mean absolute error or bias intervals.
116	A separate [post hoc supplement](POSTHOC_ERROR_INTERVALS_11-06-2026.json) computes them from the same frozen old predictions and full-precision expert targets, using task resampling and no model calls:
117	
118	| Test subset | Mean absolute error [95% interval] | Mean bias [95% interval] |
119	|---|---:|---:|
120	| All 30 files / 10 tasks | 0.201111 [0.130000, 0.273333] | +0.181111 [+0.098889, +0.262222] |
121	| Ordinary 24 files / 8 tasks | 0.230556 [0.147222, 0.304201] | +0.205556 [+0.105556, +0.294444] |
122	
123	The supplement uses the original seed and requested draw counts stated above; every sampled mean error is defined, so all draws contribute.
124	It is a new analysis of old data, not a result recorded in the historical receipt or new human evidence.
125	The old exported CSV rounds human means; the computation restores the full-precision targets from the separately hash-checked input manifest and verifies that its means and mean absolute errors match the original receipt to 1e-12.
126	No individual or per-item ratings are written into this project.
127	
128	To reproduce with access to the original private repository and a Python environment containing NumPy:
129	
130	```bash
131	python3 experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/scripts/recompute_error_intervals.py --source-repo /path/to/veribench
132	```
133	
134	The continued private paper's title is *VeriBench: An End-to-End Autoformalization Benchmark for AI Coding Agents in Lean 4*, verified in `paper_latex/TMLR_2026_VeriBench/00_main_tmlr_2026.tex` at the source commit.
135	No public bibliographic identifier was established by this import; cite these archived aggregates directly unless a public paper reference is separately verified.

| Same selected judge, ordinary-reference subset | 24 candidate files, 8 test tasks; excludes two tasks whose references were placeholders at rating time | 0.651917 [−0.166241, 0.916077] | 0.513270 [−0.201404, 0.834547] | 0.834653 [0.453743, 0.957865] |
| `104_fsc_judge_5fold_cross_validation_all_75_expert_labels`, automated recipe, primary repetition, ties preserved | All 75 files, 25 tasks, five task-disjoint folds; each scored without its task in the training fold | 0.603 [0.287, 0.836] | 0.498 | 0.621 |

Intervals are 95% percentile intervals resampling tasks, retaining their candidate files together.
Experiment 100 uses seed 20260928 and 10,000 requested draws for the full test; the ordinary subset uses 2,000 requested draws, with 1,998 nondegenerate draws for correlations and 2,000 for absolute agreement.
Experiment 104's tie-preserving addendum uses 10,000 task draws and seed 20260929.
P-values are not supplied by these imported receipts (`p-val=n/a`); no new significance test was performed.
The original aggregate CSV contains no confidence intervals; its continued-paper prose reports a Pearson interval [0.564, 0.804], but this import does not assert that it uses the later task-bootstrap method.

## The selected judge and the human target

The experiment 100 judge sees the Python source, candidate Lean file and reference Lean file at the versions shown to the human raters.
It uses their rating instructions, four conventions derived from training-split errors, and four expert-rated examples from other training tasks.
Its historical model routes are `openai/gpt-6-sol-high` with high reasoning effort and `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5-no-fallback` with maximum compute effort and adaptive thinking, through the Vals model gateway.
The score is the mean of two member medians, with three calls per member: six raw calls per completed judge score.
These are historical route identifiers, not a recommendation or authorization to run them today.

The 25 tasks were split into 10 training, 5 validation and 10 test tasks, with all three candidate files of each task kept together.
The primary target is the mean of available ratings from a panel of three experts, divided by five.
Five people supplied ratings overall; the three-expert target must not be described as uniformly three ratings per item:

| Split | Items with three expert ratings | Items with two expert ratings | Total items |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Training | 18 | 12 | 30 |
| Validation | 9 | 6 | 15 |
| Test | 18 | 12 | 30 |
| All | 45 | 30 | 75 |

These counts were computed from the source's committed input manifest without importing individual ratings.
The candidate-generation provenance traces 74 of the 75 files to `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219`, temperature 0.7, three single-call zero-shot samples per Python task, without a tool or compiler loop.
One candidate lacks a generation receipt.
Thus the three candidates are generation samples, not three different solver systems, and these data do not establish transfer to frontier coding agents.
The generation prompt allowed missing proofs; these historical files must not be relabeled as outputs of the current prove-first solver contract.

## Absolute agreement and variability

All scores here are on [0, 1].
For experiment 100's full test:

- Single-score absolute-agreement intraclass correlation, ICC(A,1): **0.727290 [0.391056, 0.890003]**.
- Consistency intraclass correlation, ICC(C,1): **0.851506**, with no interval in the imported receipt.
- Mean absolute error: **0.201111**.
- Mean bias, judge minus expert mean: **+0.181111**, from means **0.653333** and **0.472222**.
- Mean repeat standard deviation: **0.020488**; 90th percentile **0.057735**, maximum **0.173205**.

The repeat statistic is computed from three **per-pass averages of the two models**, one call per member in each pass.
It is not the variability of independent repetitions of the complete six-call, median-based judge.
This distinction is explicit in the archived ensemble code.
The imported receipt has no uncertainty intervals for mean absolute error, mean bias, or repeat standard deviation.

On the ordinary-reference subset, ICC(A,1) is **0.579786 [0.169238, 0.774305]**, mean absolute error **0.230556**, and mean bias **+0.205556** (judge **0.566667**, experts **0.361111**).
This exposes material uncertainty and score-level disagreement even though the all-item correlations are high.

## Why the new study needs fresh data

1. **Small independent task count.** The headline test has only ten task clusters; the ordinary-reference interval includes negative correlation.
2. **Reference versions and placeholder tasks.** Nine of the 25 reference files changed their theorem statements between rating and earlier judging. Five were placeholder references when rated. Experiment 100 restored rating-era inputs, but high scores on placeholder tasks contribute to its all-item correlation.
3. **Previously seen ratings.** The receipt discloses earlier exposure by experiments 75 and 83 and a descriptive initial audit. “One-shot test” refers to the selected candidate's test invocation, not a pristine dataset. The exact total number of judge versions that previously saw these ratings and the resulting selection inflation are not established by the imported receipt, explainer, or continued-paper appendix; no numerical inflation estimate is asserted.
4. **Single solver distribution.** Repeated samples from one older solver do not test transfer across agent families, tools, current model versions, or larger projects.
5. **Absolute score bias.** Correlation does not remove the positive mean bias or establish itemwise agreement.
6. **Human and judge repeat limits.** Two or three expert ratings per file and three paired-model passes provide limited evidence about conditional rating distributions and full-judge repeatability.

These limitations motivate fresh task/agent/rater splits and distribution-sensitive metrics in the new methodology.
They are not problems that disappear merely by adding more correlated ratings to the same historical items.

## Original paper versus later recipe

The original **Pearson 0.703349** row uses a separate `gpt-5.3-codex` human-rubric judge with an isotonic score mapping fit on each training fold and evaluated on the disjoint validation fold.
Its raw zero-shot Pearson value is **0.515424** on the same archived 72-item target.
Judge and mapping choices used that validation protocol; there is no independent test-set counterpart.
The source paper reports that the raw scorer package is unavailable, so this archive preserves the aggregate record rather than claiming a complete executable reproduction.

Experiment 104 evaluates an **automated recipe**, with fold-specific model-written conventions and examples and five calls per member, rather than the frozen experiment 100 judge.
Its original raw-float aggregate gives Spearman **0.601533 [0.285578, 0.834392]**, usually written **0.602**.
The published addendum rounds predictions before ranking to preserve mathematical ties and reports **0.603 [0.287, 0.836]**; use that figure when citing the continued paper.
The original excerpt is retained as provenance and must not silently overwrite the corrected figure.
The same addendum changes the second-repetition Spearman from **0.654** to **0.660**.
Its original two-repetition mean is not relabeled as a tie-corrected result.

## Artifact inventory and reproducibility

- [exp100_TEST_RECEIPT.json](exp100_TEST_RECEIPT.json): byte-exact original aggregate receipt; no per-item ratings.
- [original_cv2_aggregate_results.csv](original_cv2_aggregate_results.csv): byte-exact original aggregate results, including the 0.703349 row.
- [exp104_original_aggregate_excerpt.json](exp104_original_aggregate_excerpt.json): selected aggregate fields only; per-item arrays and other fields deliberately omitted.
- [exp104_tie_preserving_addendum.md](exp104_tie_preserving_addendum.md): byte-exact suffix extracted from the source report, explicitly labeled as an extraction in the manifest.
- [SOURCE_MANIFEST.json](SOURCE_MANIFEST.json): immutable source commit, source-file SHA-256 hashes, extraction descriptions and aggregate missingness counts.

Frozen receipts retain their original spelling and format rather than receiving new comments or terminology edits.
No candidate Lean files, reference files, individual ratings, rater identities, contact information, or new sealed ratings are included.
The source repository is private; paths and hashes document provenance without publishing its contents beyond these authorized aggregates.

## Post hoc error intervals, 11-06-2026

The historical receipt has no mean absolute error or bias intervals.
A separate [post hoc supplement](POSTHOC_ERROR_INTERVALS_11-06-2026.json) computes them from the same frozen old predictions and full-precision expert targets, using task resampling and no model calls:

| Test subset | Mean absolute error [95% interval] | Mean bias [95% interval] |
|---|---:|---:|
| All 30 files / 10 tasks | 0.201111 [0.130000, 0.273333] | +0.181111 [+0.098889, +0.262222] |
| Ordinary 24 files / 8 tasks | 0.230556 [0.147222, 0.304201] | +0.205556 [+0.105556, +0.294444] |

The supplement uses the original seed and requested draw counts stated above; every sampled mean error is defined, so all draws contribute.
It is a new analysis of old data, not a result recorded in the historical receipt or new human evidence.
The old exported CSV rounds human means; the computation restores the full-precision targets from the separately hash-checked input manifest and verifies that its means and mean absolute errors match the original receipt to 1e-12.
No individual or per-item ratings are written into this project.

To reproduce with access to the original private repository and a Python environment containing NumPy:

```bash
python3 experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/scripts/recompute_error_intervals.py --source-repo /path/to/veribench
```

The continued private paper's title is *VeriBench: An End-to-End Autoformalization Benchmark for AI Coding Agents in Lean 4*, verified in `paper_latex/TMLR_2026_VeriBench/00_main_tmlr_2026.tex` at the source commit.
No public bibliographic identifier was established by this import; cite these archived aggregates directly unless a public paper reference is separately verified.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""TLDR: Reproduce post hoc task-bootstrap error intervals from hash-checked private historical data, exporting aggregate results only."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import hashlib
import io
import json
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess

import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--source-repo", type=Path, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    manifest = json.loads((ROOT / "SOURCE_MANIFEST.json").read_text())
    source = manifest["source_files"]["cv_items"]
    data = subprocess.check_output(
        ["git", "show", manifest["source_commit"] + ":" + source["path"]],
        cwd=args.source_repo,
    )
    assert hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() == source["sha256"]
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data.decode())) if r["e100_split"] == "test"]
    target_source = manifest["source_files"]["items"]
    target_data = subprocess.check_output(
        ["git", "show", manifest["source_commit"] + ":" + target_source["path"]],
        cwd=args.source_repo,
    )
    assert hashlib.sha256(target_data).hexdigest() == target_source["sha256"]
    targets = {r["item"]: r for r in (json.loads(line) for line in target_data.splitlines() if line.strip())}
    # The old CSV rounded human targets; use the full-precision frozen targets.
    for row in rows:
        original = targets[row["item"]]
        assert original["split"] == "test" and original["task"] == row["task"]
        row["target_expert"] = original["target_expert"]
    receipt = json.loads((ROOT / "exp100_TEST_RECEIPT.json").read_text())
    result = {
        "description": "Post hoc supplement computed 11-06-2026 from frozen historical data; no new human ratings or model calls; original receipt unchanged.",
        "source_commit": manifest["source_commit"],
        "source_sha256": source["sha256"],
        "target_source_sha256": target_source["sha256"],
        "method": "95% percentile bootstrap sampling whole tasks with replacement; each sampled task retains all its candidates; seed 20260928, matching the original metric code.",
        "mean_bias_definition": "judge minus available-expert mean; positive means more lenient",
        "p_value": "n/a; descriptive intervals, no hypothesis test",
        "source_data_publication": "Aggregate statistics only; no per-item or individual human ratings included.",
        "subsets": {},
    }
    for name, subset, draws in [
        ("all_items", rows, 10000),
        ("ordinary_items", [r for r in rows if r["placeholder"].strip().lower() in ("false", "0")], 2000),
    ]:
        task_ids = sorted({r["task"] for r in subset})
        expected = receipt[name]
        assert len(subset) == expected["n_items"]
        assert len(task_ids) == expected["n_tasks"]
        pred = np.array([float(r["e100_frozen_judge"]) for r in subset])
        human = np.array([float(r["target_expert"]) for r in subset])
        error = pred - human
        values = {"mae": float(np.abs(error).mean()), "mean_bias": float(error.mean())}
        assert np.isclose(values["mae"], expected["mae"], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
        assert np.isclose(pred.mean(), expected["mean_pred"], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
        assert np.isclose(human.mean(), expected["mean_target"], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
        positions = {t: np.array([i for i, r in enumerate(subset) if r["task"] == t]) for t in task_ids}
        rng = np.random.default_rng(20260928)
        boot = {"mae": [], "mean_bias": []}
        for _ in range(draws):
            picked = rng.integers(0, len(task_ids), len(task_ids))
            index = np.concatenate([positions[task_ids[i]] for i in picked])
            boot["mae"].append(float(np.abs(error[index]).mean()))
            boot["mean_bias"].append(float(error[index].mean()))
        result["subsets"][name] = {
            "n_items": len(subset),
            "n_tasks": len(task_ids),
            "bootstrap_draws": draws,
            "mean_judge": float(pred.mean()),
            "mean_expert": float(human.mean()),
            "metrics": {
                k: {"value": values[k], "lo": float(np.percentile(v, 2.5)), "hi": float(np.percentile(v, 97.5))}
                for k, v in boot.items()
            },
        }
    output = ROOT / "POSTHOC_ERROR_INTERVALS_11-06-2026.json"
    output.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result["subsets"], indent=2))

For a **fixed finite panel** of \(H\) people with simple random sampling without replacement, use the corresponding finite-population correction \((1-m/H)s_X^2/m\) instead. Balanced assignment may require design-specific variance calculations. The chosen estimand and sampling assumptions must accompany the result.

Use uncertainty procedures that respect task groups and reused people under the actual sparse assignment. Fix the task/rater resampling or model-based analysis and check its behavior using pilot data before test inspection; do not bootstrap individual rating rows as if independent. Report an analysis conditional on the fixed panel separately from a population-of-experts analysis. With only 16 audit people, population inference can remain imprecise. The four named agents stay fixed in the primary analysis ([Owen, 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.1111)).

Secondary diagnostics are Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, Kendall tau-b, mean absolute error, and signed mean bias of expected normalized judge rating minus mean normalized human rating, with both means. Compare human-human agreement on matched artifacts. Keep model-call instability separate from predicted human disagreement: repeated probability vectors and their expected ratings need their own standard deviations and repeat counts.

Success margins, minimum improvement over baselines, maximum distribution error, maximum repeat variability, and maximum failure rate are **not yet chosen**. Set them from the intended use and a pilot that excludes final-audit people and test tasks. The planning config records these as `null`; no pass/fail conclusion is available.

## Semantic validity checks

Before scoring, specify expected changes under controlled edits and establish the relationship with checked implications or counterexamples where possible:

| Controlled edit | Expected FSC response |
|---|---|
| Remove a necessary specification obligation | Lower coverage |
| Narrow a precondition to exclude required inputs | Lower coverage of the required domain |
| Use a semantically equivalent specification | Similar coverage |
| Add irrelevant or vacuous statements | No meaningful increase |
| Supply an incomplete or faulty reference | Detect/report the discrepancy where possible |
| Change only proof completion, preserving statements | Similar coverage |

Keep these controls separate from the randomly sampled audit and report their denominators. Numeric tolerances and control counts are pending pilot decisions. Independently inspect reference defects; matching experts who share a defective reference does not establish correct FSC. Before broad collection, trace one artifact from generation through extraction, human display, judge input, probability parsing, and score computation; bind every step by content hashes. Check valid probability vectors, scale mapping, and expected responses to positive, negative, and literal-instruction controls.

## Why these counts, and what they cannot guarantee

The 64/64 training/validation tasks are a starting allocation for selecting a pretrained judge. The 768 held-out tasks preserve task coverage for the final estimate. Three ratings support an estimate of the proper loss; the additional dense ratings support conditional-distribution diagnostics. The larger number of distinct people addresses human variation that repeated work by the same few people cannot remove. Use pilot variance, learning curves, overlap, and workload to revise the allocation **before** final test inspection.

As an illustration only, a human-specific loss-effect standard deviation of 0.10 gives a normal-approximation 95% half-width contribution of \(1.96(0.10)/\sqrt{16}\approx0.049\), versus approximately 0.080 for six people. This is one hypothetical variance component, not a measured total interval. More ratings improve precision; they cannot make a biased or semantically wrong judge correct.

A fully crossed independent-identities bound or a formula in the product \(TAH\) is not a sample-size guarantee for this sparse study. Four deliberately selected systems, related tasks, and reused people violate a naive independent-rating calculation. Claims are limited to the specified benchmark, evaluated solver configurations, and justified expert population. New model versions and new populations need prospective evaluation.

## Files and next collection steps

```text
02_probabilistic_ordinal_judge/
├── README.md                  # Design and analysis contract
├── config.json                # Planned counts and unresolved choices
└── scripts/validate_design.py # Deterministic count/consistency check
```

Run `python3 experiments/02_probabilistic_ordinal_judge/scripts/validate_design.py` from the repository root. It checks this planned allocation; it does not run judges, generate ratings, or establish readiness to launch.

Next, create the private task-group manifest and rater assignment from these counts, run the training/validation pilot, set the remaining margins and budgets, and record a dated protocol amendment before collecting final-audit ratings. Each artifact record needs task/group/split IDs, stage, agent configuration ID, generation ID, Python/candidate/reference hashes, rubric hash, and judge-input hash; each rating needs its artifact ID, opaque rater ID, pool, ordinal value, timestamp, and assignment record. Each prediction needs probabilities, parsed status, judge/prompt/version IDs, repetition ID, cost receipt, and input hash. The final analysis must be reproducible from these records without exposing identities or sealed ratings in this public repository.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check the planned study's allocation and structural consistency, not launch readiness."""

import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path


def require(condition, message):
    if not condition:
        raise ValueError(message)


def pending_paths(value, prefix=""):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        for key, child in value.items():
            yield from pending_paths(child, f"{prefix}.{key}" if prefix else key)
    elif value is None:
        yield prefix


def validate(config):
    b = config["benchmark"]
    a = config["agents"]
    h = config["humans"]
    s = config["stages"]
    j = config["judge"]
    analysis = config["analysis"]
    pilot = config["pilot"]
    counts = {
        "tasks": b["tasks"],
        "train_tasks": b["train_tasks"],
        "validation_tasks": b["validation_tasks"],
        "heldout_test_tasks": b["heldout_test_tasks"],
        "agents": a["count"],
        "outputs_per_cell": a["outputs_per_task_agent_per_stage"],
        "total_people": h["total_people"],
        "training_validation_people": h["training_validation_people"],
        "final_audit_people": h["final_audit_people"],
        "base_ratings": h["base_ratings_per_artifact"],
        "dense_tasks": h["dense_tasks"],
        "dense_ratings": h["dense_total_ratings_per_artifact"],
    }
    for name, value in counts.items():
        require(type(value) is int and value > 0, f"{name} must be a positive integer")
    require(b["tasks"] == b["train_tasks"] + b["validation_tasks"] + b["heldout_test_tasks"],
            "Task splits must partition the benchmark")
    require(a["count"] == len(set(a["required_systems"])) == len(a["required_systems"]),
            "Required solver systems must be distinct and match agent count")
    require(h["total_people"] == h["training_validation_people"] + h["final_audit_people"],
            "Human pools must sum to the total people")
    require(h["disjoint_pools"] is True, "Training/validation and audit people must be disjoint")
    require(h["dense_task_source"] == "heldout_test", "Dense tasks must be held out")
    require(h["dense_tasks"] <= b["heldout_test_tasks"], "Dense subset exceeds test tasks")
    require(h["base_ratings_per_artifact"] <= h["training_validation_people"],
            "Too few training/validation people for distinct base ratings")
    require(h["base_ratings_per_artifact"] <= h["dense_total_ratings_per_artifact"] <= h["final_audit_people"],
            "Dense total must include base ratings and fit the audit pool")

    artifacts_per_task = a["count"] * a["outputs_per_task_agent_per_stage"]
    train_val_artifacts = (b["train_tasks"] + b["validation_tasks"]) * artifacts_per_task
    audit_artifacts = b["tasks"] * artifacts_per_task
    train_val_reviews = train_val_artifacts * h["base_ratings_per_artifact"]
    audit_base = audit_artifacts * h["base_ratings_per_artifact"]
    dense_extra = h["dense_tasks"] * artifacts_per_task * (
        h["dense_total_ratings_per_artifact"] - h["base_ratings_per_artifact"])
    expected = {
        "training_validation_artifacts": train_val_artifacts,
        "final_audit_artifacts": audit_artifacts,
        "total_artifacts": train_val_artifacts + audit_artifacts,
        "training_validation_reviews": train_val_reviews,
        "final_audit_base_reviews": audit_base,
        "dense_extra_reviews": dense_extra,
        "total_reviews": train_val_reviews + audit_base + dense_extra,
    }
    for name, value in expected.items():
        require(type(s[name]) is int and s[name] == value,
                f"stages.{name}: recorded {s[name]!r}, derived {value}")
    for total, people, field in [
        (train_val_reviews, h["training_validation_people"], "balanced_reviews_per_training_validation_person"),
        (audit_base + dense_extra, h["final_audit_people"], "balanced_reviews_per_final_audit_person"),
    ]:
        require(total % people == 0, f"Exact workload balance is impossible for {field}")
        require(s[field] == total // people, f"Incorrect workload in {field}")

    require(s["fresh_final_generation_for_seen_tasks"] is True,
            "Seen tasks require fresh final-audit generations")
    require(b["group_related_variants"] is True, "Related task variants must stay together")
    require(j["inputs"] == ["python_source", "candidate_lean", "gold_reference_lean"],
            "The judge must use all three declared inputs")
    require(j["rating_categories"] == list(range(6)) and j["probability_vector_length"] == 6,
            "The judge must predict all six ordinal categories")
    require(j["output"] == "probability_mass_function", "Output must be an explicit probability forecast")
    require(analysis["primary_metric"] == "normalized_ranked_probability_score"
            and analysis["primary_metric_range"] == [0, 1]
            and analysis["threshold_events"] == list(range(5)), "Invalid normalized RPS specification")
    require(analysis["weighting"] == "mean_within_artifact_then_equal_mean_across_artifacts",
            "Dense annotation must not change artifact weighting")
    require(analysis["main_judges"] == 1 and analysis["leave_one_agent_out_judges"] == a["count"],
            "Evaluate one main judge and one transfer judge per agent")
    require(analysis["transfer_test_tasks_per_agent"] == b["heldout_test_tasks"],
            "Each transfer procedure must use all held-out test tasks")

    parser.add_argument("--config", type=Path, default=Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "config.json")

content.content:
=====paper_original appendix: codex / isotonic / pass / interval / 0.703=====
10:The alignment pool contains 25 tasks (75 item keys, an item being a rated candidate file) from the human-rating collection used in Appendix~\ref{app:human_judgement_collection}.
11:The archived runs below score 72 of those 75 items, because three item keys carry no rating in the pass the run averaged; the Codex CLI runs score all 75, so the two families are not on identical items.
12:% Provenance: research_archive/experiments/results_exp16_linear_calibration/calibration_results.csv (n column: zero_shot/none/avg = 72, isotonic_cv2_tasksplit = 72, isotonic pass1->pass2 = 75, isotonic pass2->pass1 = 72). The archived NeurIPS appendix labelled every row n=75; that was wrong and is corrected here.
13:For supervised score-mapping runs, we split by \texttt{gold\_file} (task-level split, not row-level) into two folds, fit the mapping on the training fold only, and score the disjoint validation fold; the folds then swap roles and the reported value averages the two validation folds, so every task is scored exactly once as a validation task.
17:The archived CV2 task-split run of an independent \texttt{gpt-5.3-codex} judge under the human rating rubric (full files) reports cross-validated Pearson \(r=0.7033\) on the validation folds against the averaged ratings of participant~1's two earlier-prompt rating passes (one expert rater), with zero-shot \(r=0.5154\) and rank correlations \(\rho=0.3211\) and \(\tau=0.2651\); it validates that rubric judge, not the deployed Sonnet judge.
18:The raw scorer package behind that run is not part of the released artifact, and a later run of a GPT-family judge through the Codex command-line interface (CLI) used a different judge route: against the archived run's own target, participant~1's two averaged passes, its raw scores reach \(r=0.628\) zero-shot on 75 items where the archived scores reach \(r=0.5154\) on 72, so it is not a rerun of the archived scorer; against the all-rater mean its scores reach \(r=0.614\), and an isotonic mapping fit on them over the same task split gives \(r=0.2108\) against that target.
24:The acceptance thresholds date from 2026-07-23, when they were written as the bar for any replacement of the then-deployed judge, whose archived rank agreement was $0.270$: Spearman $\rho\ge0.45$ against human raters, score entropy $\ge2$ bits, modal-bin share $\le0.5$, a reference-versus-reference probe scoring $1.0$, near-zero scores for a vacuous-candidate probe, and fewer than 2\% transport failures.
26:The July text named no rater group; the expert raters were fixed as the target when the judge search below was designed, before its test-split ratings were read for the finalist.
27:Direct validation of the deployed configuration on all 25 tasks (75 items) gives expert $\rho=0.259$, $\tau=0.194$, and $r=0.139$; against the all-rater mean it gives $\rho=0.337$, $\tau=0.261$, and $r=0.266$.
28:The all-rater mean is the historical pooled target: it averages all seven rating files, including participant~1's two earlier-prompt passes, and is distinct from the five-rater reliability analysis below.
29:Its score entropy is $1.845$ bits, so it fails the agreement and entropy gates and passes the modal-share, probe, and transport gates.
31:All of them saw reference files from a September~3 snapshot rather than the versions the raters saw; Appendix~\ref{app:validated_tc_judge} repeats the search with the rated versions and reports a judge that passes.
32:% Provenance: research_archive/experiments/73_deployed_judge_human_validation/results/results_summary_2026-09-02_18-42-27.md (deployed judge); experiments/75_J1_validating_formal_spec_judge_train_val_test/results.md (gate provenance: expt-69 R2 S5, commit 801b5bb966; numbers re-verified 2026-09-08).
35:We then treated judge choice as model selection over a task-disjoint split of the 25 rated tasks: 10 training and 5 validation tasks scored only against the lenient rater group, and 10 test tasks (30 items) scored once against the expert raters.
36:The split is stratified with two test tasks per source family, and the test task set is hashed and receipt-guarded so that the finalist's expert-test evaluation ran exactly once.
37:Before that evaluation the expert ratings had been used only for the rater-agreement audit and for the direct validation of the deployed judge above, never to select a configuration.
38:The search covered three input scopes (extracted theorem blocks; both full Lean files; Python source plus both full Lean files), three rubrics (the deployed coverage rubric, the human rating rubric below, and a re-anchored coverage rubric), forward and reverse orientations, $k\in\{1,3\}$ with median or mean aggregation, \texttt{gpt-5.6-terra} as the judge model with one \texttt{gpt-5.6-sol} ceiling probe, and a prover-first hybrid.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""TLDR: Zero-call ensemble of finished judge runs on one split (mean of per-item medians; per-pass means for stability), scored with the same statistics as analyze_run.py."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import math
from statistics import median

import numpy as np

import metrics as M
from common import RESULTS, RUNS, load_items, stamp, write_json


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("runs", nargs="+")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    splits = {json.loads((RUNS / r / "manifest.json").read_text())["split"] for r in args.runs}
    assert len(splits) == 1, "all components must share one split"
    split = splits.pop()
    items = load_items(split)
    order = [i["item"] for i in items]
    by = {i["item"]: i for i in items}
    comps = []
    for r in args.runs:
        reps = {k: [] for k in order}
        for p in sorted((RUNS / r / "receipts").glob("*.json")):
            x = json.loads(p.read_text())
            if x["kind"] == "main" and x["status"] == "COMPLETE" and x["item"] in reps:
                reps[x["item"]].append((x["repeat"], x["score"]))
        comps.append({k: [s for _, s in sorted(v)] for k, v in reps.items()})
    agg = np.array([np.mean([median(c[k]) for c in comps if c[k]]) if all(c[k] for c in comps) else math.nan for k in order])
    k_min = min(len(c[k]) for c in comps for k in order)
    passes = [[float(np.mean([c[k][j] for c in comps])) for j in range(k_min)] for k in order]
    target = [by[k]["target_expert"] for k in order]
    tasks = [by[k]["task"] for k in order]
    ordinary = [n for n, k in enumerate(order) if not by[k]["ref_placeholder_at_annotation"]]
    out = {"name": args.name, "created": stamp(), "components": args.runs, "split": split, "rule": "mean of component per-item medians",
           "agreement": M.agreement(agg, target, tasks),
           "agreement_ordinary_items": M.agreement(agg[ordinary], [target[n] for n in ordinary], [tasks[n] for n in ordinary], draws=2000),
           "stability_per_pass_mean": M.repeat_stats(passes), "per_pass_spearman": M.per_pass(passes, target, M.spearman)}
    write_json(RESULTS / "ensembles" / f"{args.name}.json", out)
    g = out["agreement"]
    print(json.dumps({"name": args.name, "split": split, "spearman": g["spearman"], "ci": [g["bootstrap"]["spearman"]["lo"], g["bootstrap"]["spearman"]["hi"]],
                      "kendall": g["kendall_tau_b"], "pearson": g["pearson"], "icc_A1": g["icc_A1"], "mae": g["mae"],
                      "ordinary_spearman": out["agreement_ordinary_items"]["spearman"],
                      "mean_repeat_sd": out["stability_per_pass_mean"]["mean_repeat_sd"], "per_pass_sd": out["per_pass_spearman"]["sd"]}))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

On held-out tasks they raise Spearman from 0.570 to 0.807, and ordinary-item agreement from 0.311 to 0.606. They were never tuned on these tasks, so this is generalization rather than fit.
102:### 4.4 Rated examples and the stronger model (smaller gains)
104:- **Rated examples.** Four leave-task-out examples add little agreement (0.807 to 0.821) but halve the repeat SD (0.046 to 0.021), anchoring the score scale.
116:- **No example leakage.** The same script scans all 720 rendered H2 prompts (2,880 rated examples) and finds none from the judged task and none from a validation or test task.
126:- **Small splits.** Ten test tasks give wide intervals. A fixed judge's Spearman varies by more than 0.3 between the validation and test halves (§4 table), so ingredient comparisons use the same 45 items.
128:- **The all-items metric.** It rewards the five placeholder tasks, which every correct-input judge scores near 1. Ordinary-item agreement is therefore reported everywhere.

142:python3 ensemble.py --name <name> <sol_run> <opus_run>          # selected judge = mean of the two medians
155:  - Two causes lower train. Convention 2 scores one training candidate 0.1 where the experts gave 5/5, because its rater-era reference was a `True` placeholder. And five sorting tasks' references changed while raters were rating.
157:  - Across random 10/5/10 re-splits, one split's Spearman has SD 0.12, and a test-minus-train gap this large occurs in about one split in five.
158:  - The low repeat SD (about 0.02) is mainly the rated examples anchoring the scale (§4.4).
159:- **Cross-validated recipe (experiment 104).** An automated, task-cross-validated variant of this recipe reaches Spearman 0.603 [0.287, 0.836] over all 75 items. Each fold has its own LLM-written conventions and rated examples, and each member uses k = 5 calls. The raters' leave-one-out agreement is 0.764. This evaluates the recipe, not the frozen judge above. Its point estimate is close to the raters' instructions alone on Opus (0.600), so the hand-written conventions were a larger share of the gain than an automated writer recovers.
160:- **What it now says about VeriBench.** On the 614 tasks outside IndustrySet (experiment 102, 18,108 calls):
168:TL;DR: The judge passed because it saw the files the raters saw, used the raters' own instructions plus four conventions learned on training tasks, and anchored its scale with rated examples. Held-out ablations show the input fix and the conventions carry most of the gain; the scoreboard rubric fails even with correct inputs.

=====full workshop call text=====
Call for papers Dates Program Organizers Menu Overview Call for papers Dates Program Organizers Effective and Efficient Evaluation for AI Scientists What to measure, how to measure it, and how good th
----
-driven discovery. We organize the program by the level at which the measurement question sits, so the three areas below partition the problem. Topics of interest We welcome technical, empirical, methodological, and position papers, including work that critiques current systems and evaluation practice. What to measure Which constructs, and against what ground truth? Operational definitions of novelty, correctness, rigor, and significance, and their construct validity Ground truth stronger than reviewer opinion, such as held-out empirical outcomes and laboratory confirmation Process-level evaluation from agent execution traces How to measure it How is the instrument built? End-to-end and stage-wise benchmarks for research agents Contamination and leakage, and tasks that stay valid after training exposure LLM-as-a-judge reliability, calibration, and adversarial robustness, with cost-normalized reporting How good is the instrument How would we know the measurement holds? Reliability against validity of evaluation scores Statistical power and minimum detectable effect Sample-efficient evaluation through adaptive item selection, item response theory, best-arm identification, and off-policy reuse of prior judgments Sensitivity of rankings to judge, prompt, and rubric Also in scope, expert elicitation treated as an instrument with its own error model, reproducibility infrastructure such as execution traces, seeds, and cost logs, hazard and dual-use assessment for autonomous research in chemistry and biology, and Goodharting once a metric becomes a target. Call for papers Submissions should directly address the evaluation of autonomous scientific discovery. Papers must use the official AAAI-27 two-column author kit and be submitted as an anonymized PDF through OpenReview . Submissions that compare systems must report at matched compute and token budget, or explain why matching is infeasible. Full papers 6–8 pages Original research on evaluation methodology, benchmarking, or verification. References do not count toward the page limit. Position papers 2–4 pages Perspectives, critiques, and emerging research directions. Resource and artifact papers 2–4 pages A released benchmark, harness, corpus, or tool, submitted together with the artifact. Reviewed on whether the artifact runs and is documented. Reproduction and negative result reports 2–4 pages Attempts to reproduce published AI Scientist results, including failures. No novelty bar, judged on rigor of reporting. Submission details Format AAAI-27 two-column author kit, anonymized PDF Review Double-blind Reviews At least two per paper, a third on disagreement Proceedings Non-archival, authors retain full rights Presentation In person Relevant work under review elsewhere is welcome where the other venue permits it. At least one author of each accepted paper must register and present in person, in line with AAAI policy that virtual presentations are not permitted. All organizers attend on site. Attendance is capped at 45 to 65 participants and is by invitation on the basis of submissions, with additional AAAI-27 registrants admitted as capacity permits. Submit on OpenReview Important dates The submission deadline is 06:00 UTC, when the OpenReview portal closes. Other deadlines are 23:59 Anywhere on Earth, meaning UTC−12. 5 October 2026 Submissions open on OpenReview 20 November 2026, 06:00 UTC Submission deadline 2 December 2026 Acceptance notification 15 January 2027 Camera-ready versions due 22 February 2027 AAAI-27 workshop Program TBD Speakers IR Irina Rish Université de Montréal and Mila Evaluation that stays reliable under distribution shift. XD Xiaowu Dai University of California, Los A

findings require a declared revision of the claim or alloca-
tion rather than presenting a smaller completed subset as the
original design.

=====TMLR appendix line 13 (ambiguous window / mislinked items)=====
The reconstruction is not exact everywhere: five classical-algorithm references changed during the rating window, so the version each rater opened is unknown, and the rating sheet linked three test items (rated candidate files) to a different candidate file; excluding either group raises test agreement.
On the 24 ordinary test items, which exclude the two placeholder-reference tasks, it reaches $\rho=0.652$ with a task-bootstrap interval of $[-0.166, 0.915]$ and ICC(A,1)$=0.580$, so the gate's lower-bound requirement holds only with the placeholder items included.

name: zsh-colon-modifier-git-show
description: On this Mac (zsh), `git show $C:path` silently mangles the path via zsh's `:e`/`:h`-style modifiers; always write `${C}:path`.
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

In zsh, `git show $C:experiments/foo` expands `$C:e` as the "extension" modifier and yields `xperiments/foo`, so `git show` reports "ambiguous argument". Brace the variable: `git show "${C}:experiments/foo"`.

**Why:** Cost one wasted verification round on 11-06-2026 while reading VeriBench historical receipts at commit `be287d9b` from `/Users/brandomiranda/veribench` for the trustworthy-theorem-judges light QA.

**How to apply:** Any zsh command that concatenates a variable with `:` (git revisions, `host:path`, PATH-style lists) uses `${VAR}`. Python subprocess calls avoid the issue entirely. Related: [[ttj-historical-evidence-source]].

The review is complete. The verdict is FIXES_REQUIRED: the science and the historical numbers check out, but two process and venue items block landing as documented, and seven minor items need small edits.

# Light QA report: ordinal FSC judge methodology and AAAI-27 workshop paper

**Reviewer runtime:** Claude Fable 5.1 (`claude-fable-5-1`), effort `max`, per `../qa/dispatch.json`; read-only review, no project files edited, no model or data-collection runs. The staged state I reviewed matches all 39 hashes in `../qa/reviewed_files.json`.

## Coverage and verification results

I read every file in the manifest, the accepted GPT Pro plan, the shared rules routed by the index (Hard Rules 3, 4, 5, 10, 11; Trigger Rules 13, 77, 85), and the review-paper and terminology skills. Deterministic and source checks:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `scripts/check_project.py` (includes `validate_design.py`) | pass |
| `git diff --cached --check` on the staged tree | fails on 2 vendor lines (finding 1) |
| One-sentence-per-line on all 10 `.tex` files | pass |
| Clean `latexmk` rebuild in a scratch dir | 0 overfull boxes, 0 unresolved refs, PDF byte-identical to the staged `00_main.pdf` |
| 13 source hashes at VeriBench commit `be287d9b` (read-only `git show`) | all match `SOURCE_MANIFEST.json` |
| exp104 excerpt vs `CV_RESULTS.json`; addendum vs `results.md` suffix | all selected fields match; addendum byte-exact |
| Post hoc interval script rerun with the uv NumPy env in a scratch copy | output JSON byte-identical |
| Expert-rating availability 18/12, 9/6, 18/12 | matches `items.jsonl` |
| Generation provenance (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, T=0.7, 74 of 75 receipts, zero-shot, sorry allowed) | matches the provenance memo |
| Routes, 3-call medians, six calls per score, repeat-SD unit | match explainer, `ensemble.py`, and `freeze_and_receipt.py` line 43 (`stability_per_pass_mean`) |
| `AuthorKit27.zip`, `aaai2027.sty`, `aaai2027.bst` hashes | match the official download; preamble matches the kit template; no disallowed package used |
| Workshop call (6–8 pages, references excluded, deadline, date, double-blind, non-archival) | matches `vendor/README.md` and paper README |
| `harbor-datasets@c9dfd8e` | 896 task directories |
| RPS decomposition, strict propriety, W1 bound, noise-corrected CDF error (iid and finite panel), 0.080/0.049, √(3/8) | derived correct |
| 896/64/64/768, 512/3584/4096, 1536/10752/2560/14848, 192/832, fresh generations for seen tasks, four leave-one-agent-out fits framed as a procedure test | correct and consistent across README, config, paper |
| PDF anonymity | "Anonymous submission" header, anonymized notice, no names, handles, or URLs printed |
| Dictionary spell check of all prose | no misspellings |

## Findings, severity first

**MAJOR**

1. `[p 9/10]` **The documented landing check fails on the official style bytes.** `git diff --cached --check` reports trailing whitespace at `paper_latex/AAAI_2027_Evaluation_AI_Scientists/vendor/aaai2027.bst:11` and `vendor/aaai2027.sty:96`. Both are byte-exact kit files that `AGENTS.md:29` forbids changing, while `AGENTS.md:31` requires `git diff --check` to pass; no `.gitattributes` exists. Remedy: add a root `.gitattributes` containing `paper_latex/AAAI_2027_Evaluation_AI_Scientists/vendor/* -whitespace`, stage it, and confirm `git diff --cached --check` exits 0. Optionally assert that attribute in `scripts/check_project.py`.

2. `[p 8/10]` **Body length is below the venue's full-paper range.** The PDF is 6 pages and References begin on page 6 at line 13 of 59, so the body is about 5.2 pages. The call states full papers are 6–8 pages with references excluded, and `paper_latex/.../README.md:18` says the draft targets a full paper. Remedy: add roughly one page of substantive content before submission (candidates: a table of the four comparison conditions and what each isolates; a holdout-structure table mirroring the plan's "what each holdout establishes"; the historical human comparator and extra test caveats from finding 3; the controlled-edit table from README 02), then rebuild and recount. If a shorter category is intended instead, record that decision in the paper README.

**MINOR**

3. `[p 7/10]` **Historical comparators and limitations are incompletely carried over.** (a) The imported excerpt holds the raters' leave-one-expert-out Spearman 0.764 over all 75 artifacts and 0.747 on the 45 held-out artifacts (`exp104_original_aggregate_excerpt.json`, `human_loo_spearman`); neither `experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/README.md` nor `07_legacy_evidence.tex` reports it beside 0.826, which the judge checklist asks for when raters exist. (b) The source appendix at the manifest commit (`98_4a_appendix_validated_coverage_judge.tex`, line 13) discloses five tasks whose references changed during the rating window, so the version each rater saw is unknown (six test artifacts from two test tasks are flagged ambiguous in `items.jsonl`), and three test items whose rating sheet linked a different candidate file; excluding either raises test agreement. `README.md:75-85` and `07_legacy_evidence.tex:59` mention only the nine changed references and placeholders. Remedy: add one sentence for each caveat in both places and a human-comparator row with its denominator.

4. `[p 6/10]` **Bias sign convention is not stated in the paper.** `01_abstract.tex:12` and `07_legacy_evidence.tex:38,46` give +0.181 and +0.206 with both means but never say "judge minus expert mean, positive is lenient"; `README.md:64` and the post hoc JSON do. Remedy: define it once at `07_legacy_evidence.tex:38` and add "judge minus expert" in the abstract.

5. `[p 6/10]` **Proof visibility for the main study is not stated.** `AGENTS.md:14` requires stating exactly which proof bodies are visible; `03_target.tex:11` only says it is "recorded separately", and README 02 line 93 says byte-identical contents. Remedy: one sentence in `03_target.tex` and README 02 item 5 stating that raters and the judge both see the complete candidate and reference files, including any proof bodies or `sorry` placeholders, with proof completion recorded as a separate variable.

6. `[p 5/10]` **Terminology drift against Rule 85 and `AGENTS.md:25`.** People: the paper uses expert(s) 25 times, people 9, participant(s) 5, rater(s) 9, person 2 (for example `05_design.tex:15-17,29,73`, `06_inference.tex:7,12,18,19,48`, `09_discussion.tex:7`); README 02 uses "people" 21 times. Solvers: the paper uses solver configuration(s), configuration(s), solver, and agent(s); README 02 mostly "agent", also "systems"; `config.json` keys say agents. Ratings versus reviews: `05_design.tex:29`, `06_inference.tex:18`, README 02 lines 76-85, `config.json` stage keys. Dictionary words from the terminology skill: "cell" (`05_design.tex:22-23`, README 02 line 72), "frozen/freeze" (`05_design.tex:8,69,72`, `07_legacy_evidence.tex:40,64`, `09_discussion.tex:14`), "protocol" (abstract line 15, `02_introduction.tex:29`, `03_target.tex:22`, `08_controls_reporting.tex:37`), "files" for artifacts at `05_design.tex:40`. Remedy: choose rater, solver configuration, rating, artifact; apply across the paper, both READMEs and the root README; keep `config.json` keys or rename them together with `validate_design.py`.

7. `[p 5/10]` **Judge-recipe gaps (Rule 77).** The planned baselines at `06_inference.tex:61` and README 02 line 112 include no non-LLM baseline and no label-reproduction test, although the historical record shows a one-line theorem-count ratio beat every earlier LLM judge. Remedy: add a theorem-count-ratio baseline expressed in the six-category format and a label-in-prompt reproduction test to the pilot list in README 02 and `05_design.tex` "Pilot and frozen execution".

8. `[p 4/10]` **Anonymity check and bibliography hygiene.** `scripts/check_project.py:38` asserts the literal "Anonymous Submission" in `00_main.tex`, but the rendered header comes only from `\usepackage[submission]{aaai2027}` (`vendor/aaai2027.sty:35-37,135`); the assertion would pass even if the option were dropped. `references.bib:34` embeds a GitHub handle in the url field; the official `.bst` does not print url for `@misc`, so the PDF is clean, but any source upload would leak it. Remedy: assert the `[submission]` option in `check_project.py`; drop the url field and keep the commit hash in the note.

9. `[p 3/10]` **Document-header and public-prose hygiene.** `experiments/01_legacy_veribench_judge/README.md:1` and `vendor/README.md:1` put an HTML comment before the H1 unlike the other READMEs (Rule 16 wants the title first). `README.md:13-14` ("The remembered correlations around '0.6, 0.8, 0.8'...") is a private note inside a public file. Remedy: move or delete the comments; rewrite lines 13-14 as a neutral disambiguation of the three experiment-100 statistics, or delete them.

## Remaining limitations and notes, not counted

- `07_legacy_evidence.tex` quotes six-decimal values in prose while its table uses three; three decimals in prose would suffice, receipts keep full precision.
- Three underfull boxes exist (the paragraph at `07_legacy_evidence.tex:55-61`, badness 4441, and two in the bibliography); the build rule allows them.
- The paper does not say how the six probabilities are elicited (verbalized, log-probability, or sampling-based) or the fitted-mapping family. Consistent with the pending status, but reviewers will ask.
- The continued private paper's own caption describes the repeat SD as per-model SDs averaged, which contradicts the archived code; the new README is right. A one-line note of that discrepancy in README 01 would pre-empt confusion.
- README 02 cites Owen 2007 while the paper cites Owen and Eckles 2012; both are valid, align if desired.
- I did not visually re-inspect rendered pages; I verified text, page count, and byte identity with a clean rebuild. Pending human data and unset thresholds are treated as intended limitations, not defects.

## Ranked next steps

- `[p 9/10]` Add the `.gitattributes` exemption and re-run `git diff --cached --check`, since the documented landing check currently fails.
- `[p 8/10]` Decide the page-length route (add content or declare the category) before the 11-20-2026 06:00 UTC deadline.
- `[p 7/10]` Carry the human comparator and the two extra test caveats into README 01 and section 7, then rebuild and recommit the PDF.
- `[p 5/10]` Do the terminology pass and the small statement fixes (bias sign, proof visibility) in one edit, then rerun `check_project.py`.

VERDICT: FIXES_REQUIRED
CRITICAL_ISSUES: 0
MAJOR_ISSUES: 2
MINOR_ISSUES: 7

**TLDR-end:** [ttj: light QA of the ordinal FSC judge methodology, historical import, and AAAI-27 workshop paper] The math, counts, hashes, recompute, kit, and anonymity all verify, but landing is blocked until the vendor whitespace exemption is added and the 5.2-page body versus the 6–8-page full-paper rule is resolved, plus seven minor edits.
